papers.id_or_url: arXiv 2411.16353 (Balesni, Korbak, Evans; titled 'The Two-Hop Curse', later 'Lessons from Studying Two-Hop Latent Reasoning', v4 Nov 2025)
papers.title: Lessons from Studying Two-Hop Latent Reasoning
papers.key_idea: Fine-tuned models compose two facts latently without CoT only when both facts sit in the same document or prompt. Facts in separate documents give chance-level no-CoT two-hop accuracy (the 'two-hop curse'). v4: failure is not only synthetic; synthetic+natural pairs can succeed; frontier models fail no-CoT two-hop in over half of question categories (from snippet).
papers.result: Chance-level two-hop no-CoT when facts are in separate docs; CoT recovers most categories.

papers.id_or_url: arXiv 2402.16837 (Yang, Kassner, Gribovskaya, Riedel, Geva; Findings ACL 2025)
papers.title: Do Large Language Models Latently Perform Multi-Hop Reasoning?
papers.key_idea: Pretrained LLMs latently compose facts; shortcut explanations via co-occurrence of head and answer entities in training sequences are a confound for some relation types.
papers.result: Latent two-hop used in >80% of prompts for certain relation types (from snippet); co-occurrence shortcuts noted.

papers.id_or_url: https://neurips.cc/virtual/2026/170471 (OpenReview forum dPo7MFIbmu; no arXiv id found)
papers.title: Anchoring the Bridge Across Hops: Unlocking Latent Multi-Hop Reasoning under Knowledge Injection (BRACE)
papers.key_idea: Diagnoses a bridge-entity representation mismatch between hops after knowledge injection; BRACE reuses one shared descriptor pool for the bridge entity in both hops so the two hop representations align. Targets composition of updated facts where no training sample contains both hops.
papers.result: Reported 3-31% relative gain over strongest rewriting baseline across four LLMs from 1.7B to 14B (from abstract summary). CoT and composition demos do not reliably help latent composition; prompting lowered composed accuracy under 3 of 4 rewrites.

papers.title: Knowledge-Instruct: Effective Continual Pre-training from Limited Data using Instructions (Ovadia et al., Microsoft)
papers.key_idea: Converts small raw corpora into synthetic instruction-response pairs and trains only on those, avoiding continual-pretraining forgetting; synthetic data may come from relatively small models; claims gains on multi-hop and retrieval integration. Releases 'Companies' injection benchmark.
papers.result: Abstract claims better factual memorization and less forgetting than CPT; no numbers verified (abstract only).

papers.title: Comparing Knowledge Injection Methods for LLMs in a Low-Resource Regime (Abonizio et al.)
papers.key_idea: Plain continued pretraining on small data helps modestly; exposing the model to diverse textual variations (paraphrase-style augmentation) helps much more; models can generate their own effective synthetic training data.

gaps_nobody_solved: No paper tests two-hop composition of facts learned on different days, across sequential training sessions, with a KL-anchored or LoRA update. All cited results use one-shot full fine-tuning or CPT on a single corpus.

The two-hop curse (2411.16353) is shown with separate documents, but no method has been shown to fix it at 3-4B under a fixed small training budget. BRACE (1.7B-14B) is the nearest, but its gains are reported relative to rewriting baselines, not absolute, and its code and training budget were not verified.

Interaction between nightly replay/dreaming (generated bridge-entity data) and composition is unstudied. Multi-hop composition is never measured after the model has been further trained on unrelated days (forgetting of the bridge link).

Learning from mistakes and abstention (knowing when to ask) are not addressed by any of the knowledge-injection papers above; they are only studied in RL/skill-training settings like 2603.02091, not on fact composition.
Reversal curse and two-hop curse are studied separately; no paper evaluates both together in the same small model, which matters because two-hop queries often need reverse lookup.
Speed with several agents (30+ tok/s on a laptop) is outside the scope of the knowledge-injection literature; no found paper links composition quality to KV-cache or decode-speed tradeoffs.

Most cited results come from abstracts or search summaries; numbers for 2504.05571, 2508.06178 and 2602.02470 were not checked in full text. Two of ten pages were fetched (the BRACE NeurIPS listing and the Knowledge-Instruct abstract); the rest are from search snippets.

papers.title: AgentHER: Hindsight Experience Replay for LLM agent trajectory relabeling
papers.key_idea: Relabels failed agent runs with an alternative goal so the failure becomes a correct demonstration; outputs SFT and DPO data. Offline replay of failures, no online loop.
papers.result: Per search snippets only (not verified by reading): gains over success-only SFT on WebArena and ToolBench; reports matching baseline with 50% of successful demos; +2.1 pp over extra redeployment rounds. One aggregator says no independent reproduction yet.

papers.title: Agent-R: iterative self-training so agents reflect and recover from errors (MCTS-built correction data)
papers.key_idea: MCTS finds the first wrong step in a trajectory and splices in a corrected continuation; the model is trained on recovery trajectories. Closest match to learning recovery from own errors in weights.
papers.result: Per snippet: about +5.59% over baselines across three interactive environments. Not verified.

papers.title: Trial and Error: Exploration-Based Trajectory Optimization of LLM Agents (ETO)
papers.key_idea: Iterative loop: agent collects failure trajectories, then trains on contrastive failure-vs-success pairs (DPO-style). Foundational method for DPO from agent failures.
papers.result: Snippet-level only; the foundational baseline for preference learning on agent failures.

papers.title: Experiential Reflective Learning for Self-Improving LLM Agents
papers.key_idea: Training-free: reflects on single-attempt experiences and stores transferable heuristics that are reused at inference. Explicitly argues fine-tuning is costly, so it is the no-weights alternative to a nightly loop.
papers.result: Per snippet: +7.8% success over ReAct on Gaia2. Workshop paper (ICLR 2026 MemAgents). Not verified.

papers.title: SENTINEL: Failure-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Training Tool-Using LM Agents
papers.key_idea: RL trains on the solver's own failure modes (e.g., wrong item grounding, missing actions) rather than generic tasks. Failure-targeted training on tau2-bench Retail.
papers.result: Per snippet: Pass^1 66.4 to 74.9 on tau2 Retail, vs 69.0 for a general RL baseline. LoRA not confirmed. Not verified.

papers.title: Self-Evolution for Multi-Turn Tool-Calling Agents via Divergence-Point Preference Learning
papers.key_idea: Finds the divergence point where a trajectory first goes wrong and builds preference pairs there (local DPO signal rather than whole-trajectory). Tracks error types (duplicate actions, missing args, low reward).
papers.result: Evaluated on tau2-bench retail and other domains with Qwen3.5-9B base (larger than the 3-4B target). Not verified.

papers.title: FC-SWE: failed-patch feedback as context for a recovery trajectory (GRPO-based)
papers.key_idea: After a failed verification, restores the repo and feeds the failed patch plus verifier output as context for a recovery attempt; trains on these failure-recovery trajectories. Uses GRPO, not DPO.
papers.result: Snippet: Qwen3.5-4B + SWE-agent, Resolved@1 41.7% vs 38.9% for GRPO baseline. Title link inferred from search snippet; verify before citing.

papers.title: Fine-tuning a retrospective (reflection) model for agents
papers.key_idea: Fine-tunes a small model to write reflections on past failed steps, instead of prompting a large model to reflect at inference; reflections then guide the agent.
papers.result: Snippet: significantly beats reflection-prompting baselines on TravelPlanner, NATURAL PLAN, tau-bench. Not verified.

papers.title: Self-play SWE-RL (SSR): agent injects bugs and solves them, failed repairs become higher-order bugs
papers.key_idea: Single LLM self-play: bug-injection and bug-solving roles trained by RL; the solver's failed repairs feed the next round. Self-generated curriculum from failures.
papers.result: Snippet: +10.4 SWE-bench Verified, +7.8 SWE-Bench Pro. Needs a code sandbox; large-model scale in paper.

papers.title: Sequential single-LoRA continual learning (SLAO; SLoRA noise filtering)
papers.key_idea: Relevant to the nightly-training failure mode: one persistent LoRA updated sequentially with orthogonal init and time-aware merging (SLAO); SLoRA filters noisy LoRA components by subspace similarity to the base to reduce forgetting. Neither targets agents.
papers.result: SLoRA: up to 12% accuracy gain, 29% less forgetting (snippet). SLAO: beats data-free CL baselines. Not agent-specific.

gaps_nobody_solved: No found paper trains a 3-4B model nightly on its own day-logs with a KL anchor and measures recall or failure fixes across nights. All work is single-shot or multi-round in a benchmark loop.
DPO/KTO on real deployment failures with human-free grading: the found work uses environment rewards or a teacher (Claude API) for labels; grading noise and label drift over nights are not studied.
Joining facts (two-hop) learned from an agent's own failures: none of the papers address whether failure-based fixes transfer across hops in weights.
Long-task memory via weights: all found methods keep failure lessons in prompts/memory (ERL, IBM 2603.10600) or in short tau-bench-style episodes; none tests weight-stored lessons over weeks.

Knowing when to ask or abstain after learning from mistakes: Abstain-R1 (2604.17073), Agentic Abstention (2606.28733), AgentAbstain (2607.10059) are evaluations or question-answering RL; none combine failure-driven training with abstention on tool-use agents at small scale.
Interference between nightly failure-fix updates and previously learned skills (retail tool-call skill vs. new fixes) under a fixed KL anchor is not measured in any found agent paper.
Speed under several concurrent agents on a laptop: none of the papers address serving cost of per-agent adapters for 30+ tok/s parallel agents.

Verification of the snippet-only numbers: AgentHER, SENTINEL, divergence-point, FC-SWE and Agent-R results were taken from search snippets and were not checked against the full papers; no fetches were used.

papers.title: MEM1: Learning to Synergize Memory and Reasoning for Efficient Long-Horizon Agents
papers.key_idea: RL-trained agent keeps one shared internal state (<IS>) refreshed each turn from prior state + new observation; earlier turns are discarded so context stays constant. Memory efficiency is not rewarded directly; it emerges from task-success reward.
papers.result: Abstract claims MEM1-7B ~3.5x performance and ~3.7x lower memory vs Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct on 16-objective multi-hop QA; figures from secondary summaries, not checked in full text. Relevance: constant-memory agent for a 7B-class model; the state is the scratchpad a laptop agent would carry.

papers.title: MEM AGENT: Reshaping Long-Context LLM with Multi-Conv RL-based Memory Agent
papers.key_idea: Reads long input in chunks and maintains a fixed-length rolling memory that is overwritten each step; trained end-to-end with RL (DAPO extension, independent-context multi-conversation generation). Released RL-MemAgent-7B and 14B.
papers.result: v1 abstract: 8K-trained model extrapolates to 3.5M-token QA with <5% loss and 95%+ on 512K RULER. ICLR 2026 version softens to <10% loss. Numbers differ by version; check latest. Relevance: overwrite-memory pattern is a candidate for per-agent working memory with fixed token budget.

papers.title: Mem-alpha: Learning Memory Construction via Reinforcement Learning
papers.key_idea: Agent learns what to write, where (core / episodic / semantic stores) and when to update, via tool calls; reward = downstream QA accuracy over full interaction history. Replaces hand-written memory rules.
papers.result: Secondary summary: trained on ~30K-token instances, generalizes to >400K-token test sequences. Not verified against paper. Relevance: directly about the 'what to keep' decision a nightly learner would need.

papers.title: Memory-R1: Enhancing LLM Agents to Manage and Utilize Memories via Reinforcement Learning
papers.key_idea: Two RL-tuned agents (Memory Manager picks ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP; Answer Agent filters then reasons over memories), PPO/GRPO, outcome reward only.
papers.result: Abstract: SOTA on LoCoMo with only 152 training QA pairs; models 3B-14B. ACL 2026 long paper.

papers.title: Do Language Models Need Sleep? Offline Recurrence for Improved Online Inference
papers.key_idea: Periodically runs extra offline recurrent passes over stored context and writes it into fast weights of SSM blocks via a learned local rule, then clears the KV cache; wake-time latency unchanged. More sleep passes helped, most on deeper reasoning.
papers.result: Tested on synthetic tasks (cellular automata, multi-hop graph retrieval) and a math task; transformer and SSM-attention hybrids struggled. Relevance: the fast-weight mechanism needs SSM/recurrent blocks, so it maps to the Qwen3.6 Gated DeltaNet layers but not directly to plain-attention K2-Horizon. Not confused with Behrouz et al. 'Language models need sleep' (relation unverified).

papers.title: Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time (Letta, Lin et al.)
papers.key_idea: Agent uses idle time to rewrite/pre-compute its memory state (context) so less reasoning is needed at query time.
papers.result: Reported on AIME/GSM-style math; load moved off user-facing requests without quality loss (per Letta blog). Id is the known-ids entry (verified by grep only, not fetched).

papers.title: Remember Me, Refine Me: Dynamic Procedural Memory Framework (ReMe)
papers.key_idea: Procedural memory lifecycle: distillation, context-adaptive reuse, utility-based pruning, so memory is refined rather than an append-only archive.
papers.result: Per abstract: Qwen3-8B agent with ReMe beats memoryless Qwen3-14B on BFCL-V3 and AppWorld. Relevance: a skill/procedure store that is pruned by utility, which fits a nightly skill-sleep pipeline.

papers.title: ProcMEM: Learning Reusable Procedural Memory from Experience via Non-Parametric PPO
papers.key_idea: Turns episodic experience into executable skills with activation, execution and termination conditions; non-parametric PPO with a verification gate; no weight updates.
papers.result: Abstract-level only. Relevance: a way to write verified skills without touching weights, a no-training baseline for skill-sleep.

papers.title: CompactionRL: context compaction inside the RL loop
papers.key_idea: Jointly trains task execution and summary generation so the policy learns what to keep when context is compacted.
papers.result: Claims GLM-4.5-Air (106B-A30B) Pass@1 66.8% SWE-bench Verified, 24.5% Terminal-Bench 2.0. Large model; small-model transfer unknown. Related: SUPO (ACL 2026, 'Beyond the Context Window', summarization-augmented policy optimization, arXiv id not found in search).

papers.title: Toward Reliable Context Compression for Long-Horizon Agents: An Empirical Study of Execution Instability
papers.key_idea: Argues compression should keep what supports future actions, not a faithful transcript; examines execution instability under compaction; notes TACO-RL optimizes prompt compression but only for static prompts and single-shot outputs.
papers.result: Empirical study (abstract only read). Relevance: warns that summary-based compaction can make agents unstable, a failure mode to test on a 3-4B model.

papers.title: CONTRAMEM: Learning Self-Evolving Procedural Memory from Contrasting Multi-Model Trajectories
papers.key_idea: Builds procedural memory from contrasting trajectories across several models to avoid blind-spot inheritance from one policy's own memory.
papers.result: Abstract only. Relevance: contrastive (good vs bad) trajectories for memory, close to fixed-failure/DPO data in the skill-sleep plan.

gaps_nobody_solved: No published test of nightly weight consolidation (LoRA + KL anchor) on a 3-4B model with the logs of a single user; the sleep papers (2605.26099, 2504.13171) use synthetic tasks or math, not a laptop assistant.
Joining facts (two-hop) during sleep or memory writing: none of the memory-agent papers measure two-hop recall from weights; MEM1/MemAgent/Mem-alpha test QA over retrieved or in-context memory.

Learning from mistakes that persists across sessions without retraining: ProcMEM/ReMe/CONTRAMEM store procedures in context, and no paper compares in-context procedure stores against weight-based DPO/KTO fixes on the same tasks.
Knowing when to ask or abstain: no memory paper in this set reports abstention or clarification rates as a metric.
Multi-agent memory on one laptop: none of the papers measure throughput (tok/s) with several agents sharing a memory or KV budget, under a fixed unified-memory limit.
Compaction stability at small scale: 2608.06503 reports instability, but no found method is shown to keep a 3-4B model stable over long tool-use runs (30+ turns) with a fixed token budget.
Forgetting control: none of these methods reports what happens to previously learned facts after many nightly updates (the 'sleep' papers report single-pass or few-pass gains, not multi-night drift).

papers.title: Persistent Q4 KV Cache for Multi-Agent LLM Inference on Apple Silicon
papers.key_idea: Block pool giving each agent an isolated Q4-quantized KV cache that persists across restarts; targets multi-agent serving on Apple Silicon. Compares against vllm-mlx; Q4 warm-cache TTFT reported to match FP16 prefix cache while surviving restarts and memory pressure.
papers.result: Per search snippet: Q4 warm TTFT ~ FP16 prefix-cache latency; FP16 cache fails under memory pressure. Not verified against full paper.

papers.title: Native LLM and MLLM Inference at Scale on Apple Silicon
papers.key_idea: MLX-based engine with continuous batching and prefix caching. Reports 5.8x speedup on shared prompt prefixes.
papers.result: 5.8x on shared prefixes (self-reported in snippet).

papers.title: KVFlow: Efficient Prefix Caching for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Workflows (NeurIPS 2025)
papers.key_idea: Agent Step Graph gives each agent a steps-to-execution value that drives node-level eviction in a radix/tree prefix cache; background CPU->GPU prefetch for agents scheduled next. Replaces LRU.
papers.result: Authors: up to 1.83x single-workflow, up to 2.19x with many concurrent workflows vs SGLang hierarchical radix cache. GPU serving, not Apple Silicon. A 2026 critique (PBKV) says it assumes a predefined step graph.

papers.title: Efficient Serving for Dynamic Agent Workflows with Prediction-based KV-Cache Management (PBKV)
papers.key_idea: Prediction-based KV-cache management for dynamic agent workflows with runtime-dependent loops, addressing KVFlow's fixed-graph assumption.
papers.result: Not read; from search listing only.

papers.title: Specter: Fast MoE Inference via Quantization-Enabled Multi-Step Speculative Offloading
papers.key_idea: Quantized draft model plus expert prefetching so expert transfers overlap with drafting and verification; single-GPU MoE offloading.
papers.result: Authors: avg 1.50x TPOT speedup for single-request, peak 1.88x, vs prior SOTA offloading system (self-reported, not checked).

papers.title: DraftExpert: Expansion-Aware Self-Speculative Decoding for End-Device MoE Inference
papers.key_idea: Self-speculative decoding for single-user MoE on end devices; argues expert loading (not arithmetic) is the decode bottleneck, so speculation value depends on how many new experts each step pulls in. Target-expert prefetching.
papers.result: Abstract: 'improves decode throughput by 1.45x on average.' Baseline not named in abstract. A Pith summary's claim that the baseline lacks caching is secondary and unverified. Treat 1.45x as unanchored.

papers.title: Accelerating MoE Inference by Hiding Offloading Latency with Speculative Decoding (SpecMoEOff)
papers.key_idea: Speculative decoding enlarges per-expert workload so GPU/CPU offloaded-expert work is balanced and offload latency is hidden.
papers.result: Not checked numerically.

papers.title: The Limits of Speculation: Bounding Speculative Decoding in Mixture-of-Experts
papers.key_idea: Bounds on speculative decoding gains for MoE because verification of k tokens activates more experts; experiments on A100.
papers.result: Limits claim, not a speedup. Relevant to whether spec decoding helps a 3B-active MoE on a laptop.

papers.title: SpecStream: Resource-Efficient Speculative Decoding for Long-Context LLM Serving
papers.key_idea: Starts verification before full KV history is restored; overlaps drafting with KV transfer during offloading.
papers.result: Authors: 1.41x and 1.32x throughput over offloading baseline (Qwen3, InternLM2.5). GPU serving.

papers.title: D-cut: Adaptive Verification Depth Pruning for Batched Speculative Decoding
papers.key_idea: Shows batched spec decoding throughput saturates and falls below AR at bs=64; prunes verification depth adaptively. High MAT does not imply high throughput.
papers.result: Qualitative from snippet; key warning for several-agent concurrency.

papers.title: NebulaSD: Many-for-Many Speculative Decoding
papers.key_idea: Shared draft and target model pools with batches rebuilt across them to avoid fixed draft-target pairing waits under high concurrency.
papers.result: 4-GPU prototype gains (snippet only).

papers.title: H-Spec: Parallel Speculative Decoding Without a Drafter-Side KV Cache
papers.key_idea: Drafter with no KV cache, lowering KV utilization for 8-128 concurrent requests under vLLM.
papers.result: Highest throughput and lowest KV utilization per authors (snippet only).

papers.title: Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories
papers.key_idea: Two-stage sleep pipeline moving knowledge from fast modules to slow durable ones; more consolidation stages keep improving; retains prior knowledge across sequential exposures.
papers.result: Authors' claims per snippet; not verified. Closest published analogue to Premonition's nightly sleep.

gaps_nobody_solved: No published method for expert-level caching of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-class Gated DeltaNet hybrid MoE on a 32 GB laptop with several concurrent agents; prefix caching breaks for DeltaNet recurrent state (zolotukhin.ai 2026-05-07 blog, not a paper).
Batched speculative decoding loses its benefit at high concurrency (D-cut); no result for 3-4B models with 3-6 agents on Apple Silicon with mixed-length agent batches.
Shared prefix reuse across agents whose prompts differ by one tool-result is unsolved for recurrent (DeltaNet) layers; KV-only prefix caches do not transfer.
Speculative decoding on Apple Silicon/MLX with multiple concurrent agents: no paper found; all spec-decoding serving results are GPU.
Abstain/ask-when-unsure in small on-device agents: search found no 2026 paper with eval; only industry cascade guides (confidence-gated escalation, unevaluated).
Nightly on-device LoRA with KL anchor and re-read/dream replay: no paper evaluates the full loop; sleeping-llm (GitHub) and Medium posts only.
Learning from mistakes and two-hop fact joining under nightly updates: no retrieved 2025-2026 method addresses it in small models with a sleep loop.
Small-model MCP tool-call reliability on CPU: arXiv 2609.07370 exists (sub-2B benchmark) but snippet only showed references; unverified.

papers.title: Abstain-R1: Calibrated Abstention and Post-Refusal Clarification via Verifiable RL
papers.key_idea: RLVR with a clarification-aware reward: reward correct answers on answerable queries; on unanswerable queries reward explicit abstention plus a post-refusal clarification semantically aligned with the missing info. Evaluated on Abstain-Test, Abstain-QA, SelfAware.
papers.result: shown (abstract fetch): 3B model; claims substantial gain over its base on unanswerable queries, keeps answerable accuracy, competitive with DeepSeek-R1. No numbers on the abstract page. Limitations not stated there. Prompting helps large models far more than small ones (search snippet, unverified in full text). Closest match to the laptop-size target. Transferable as data recipe (generate unanswerable + clarification targets) without online RL.

papers.title: AgentAbstain: Do LLM Agents Know When Not to Act?
papers.key_idea: Benchmark/framework for tool-using agents deciding whether to act vs abstain or ask when required arguments are missing or the task is underspecified; notes agents tend to fabricate missing arguments rather than ask.
papers.result: shown (search snippet): best of 17 frontier models reaches 59.5% paired accuracy; abstention argued to be largely independent of general task-solving ability. Frontier models only; no small-model results seen.

papers.title: Ask or Assume? Uncertainty-Aware Clarification-Seeking in Coding Agents
papers.key_idea: Studies when coding agents should ask for clarification versus assume, with calibration of the decision to ask.
papers.result: shown (snippet): authors say findings may not carry over to smaller open-weight models. Directly flags the small-model gap.

papers.title: When and How Should an Agent Clarify? CIGAsk: Teaching LLMs to Clarify via Counterfactual Information Gain
papers.key_idea: Trains a policy to decide whether to clarify and how to phrase the question, rewarded by counterfactual information gain; motivated by models committing to one interpretation and answering confidently wrong.
papers.result: suggested/unverified (snippet only). Likely needs simulated users for reward; check for small-model results.

papers.title: Knowing When to Ask: Self-Gated Clarification for Hierarchical Language Agents (ActionRating)
papers.key_idea: Puts clarification into the agent action space so it competes with acting at every decision point, instead of rating final answers or sampling agreement.
papers.result: shown (snippet): evaluated on hierarchical classification, not open-ended tool use. Self-gating idea is a candidate for a cheap per-step ask-vs-act head on a small model.

papers.title: Structured Uncertainty guided Clarification for LLM Agents (SAGE-Agent)
papers.key_idea: Scores candidate clarification questions by Expected Value of Perfect Information over a structured uncertainty model; penalizes redundant questions.
papers.result: shown (snippet): 7-39% higher coverage of ambiguous tasks and 1.5-2.7x fewer clarification questions than baselines. Structured-uncertainty approach is a template for asking fewer, better questions.

papers.title: Search, Do not Guess: Teaching Small Language Models to Be Effective Search Agents
papers.key_idea: Argues small models cannot reliably decide when to search from their own confidence (the adaptive-search trap); proposes an always-search policy trained by fine-tuning on grounded retrieval-based answers.
papers.result: shown (abstract fetch): adaptive search degrades SLM performance; SLMs invoke search less often and hallucinate more; fine-tuned SLMs gain +17.3 on Bamboogle and +15.3 on HotpotQA over agent distillation from LLMs. Key counter-evidence against adaptive look-up gating in small models. Name 'Adaptive Search Trap' came from snippet; abstract shows the claim without that label.

papers.title: TIAR: Trajectory-Informed Advantage Reweighting for LLM Abstention Learning
papers.key_idea: RL that marks questions the model cannot solve across sampled responses as out-of-knowledge, and reweights advantages for abstention.
papers.result: snippet only. Already in known-ids.

papers.title: Rewarding Efficient Reasoning Improves Abstention on Underspecified Tasks in Reasoning Models
papers.key_idea: Reward shaping for efficient reasoning to improve abstention on underspecified tasks in reasoning models.
papers.result: snippet only. Already in known-ids.

papers.title: Ask Early, Ask Late, Ask Right: When Does Clarification Timing Matter for Long-Horizon Agents?
papers.key_idea: Studies whether the timing of clarification questions matters in long-horizon agent tasks.
papers.result: snippet only. Relevant to long-task memory plus when-to-ask. Not checked for small models.

papers.title: Knowledge-boundary abstention SFT/DPO family (Purging the Gray Zone; KARL; honest VLM knowledge boundaries)
papers.key_idea: Standard recipe: label answerable vs unanswerable from the model's own correctness, then SFT or DPO toward 'I don't know' (R-Tuning lineage).
papers.result: snippet only. Good fit for nightly self-labelled abstention data from the model's own dream/eval logs. Note 2506.09038 (in known-ids) found reasoning fine-tuning cut abstention about 24%.

gaps_nobody_solved: No study tests whether abstention or clarification behaviour survives repeated small LoRA updates (nightly sleep loop, KL-anchored). Forgetting of abstention under continual fine-tuning is unmeasured.

Small (3-4B) models: most ask/abstain papers use frontier or 7B+ models; Abstain-R1 (3B) is the main exception, and Ask-or-Assume explicitly says its results may not transfer to small open-weight models.

Self-knowledge is too weak for gating look-ups in small models: 'Search, Do not Guess' reports adaptive search degrades SLMs. Utilization is also a bottleneck: 2603.11513 reports models <=7B fail to extract the answer 85-100% of the time even with oracle retrieval on questions they cannot answer alone (snippet). Joint ask / look-up / act policy for small models is not solved.
Learning from the user's answers to clarifying questions as a nightly training signal (ask -> user answer -> SFT or DPO) is not studied; CIGAsk-type work uses simulated users.
Per-user ask frequency calibration (how often this person wants questions vs. acting) learned from feedback over time is not addressed in these papers.

Irreversible-action gating (send email, delete file, book event) for small agents with a KV/throughput budget: clarification latency cost at 30+ tok/s with several concurrent agents is not modelled in any paper found.
Abstention for multi-hop joining facts (two-hop) and for learning from mistakes is not covered by the ask/abstain literature found; the closest is 2604.04651 for search, not for internal fact joins.

candidates.name: Alias-to-Entity State Tying (ASTie)
candidates.one_line: At night, train the LoRA so the mid-layer hidden state at the end of a description ('my sister', 'the guy who fixes the boiler') matches the hidden state at the entity's own name ('Maya'). Facts stored under the name then fire from the description, so two-hop joins should work for pairs that were never dreamed together.
candidates.mechanism: STORED: the same nightly LoRA as ab_ob_b4_nb (attention + MLP, all layers). Nothing new at serve time. NIGHT: (1) The tagger and names pass already give (alias, entity) links from the day's logs, e.g. 'my sister' -> 'Maya'. Only links seen at least twice, or confirmed by Ben's own words, are used; fake names from the names pass such as 'Sister' are filtered by a blocklist of kinship and role words. (2) For each link, build probe pairs that differ only in the entity slot (P_alias = "Ben's sister's", P_name = "Maya's"), each with 3-6 fixed relation-neutral suffixes ('__ phone number is', '__ job is'). (3) Stop-grad forward on P_name; read the residual at the last entity token at layers La..Lb (about 25-45% depth, roughly layers 9-16 of 36 on K2-3.7B, chosen by the patching scan below). (4) Add L_tie = mean over those layers of (1 - cos(h_alias, sg(h_name))) plus a small norm MSE to the recall + KL-anchor loss, weight lambda in {0.1, 0.3} swept once on a dev world. Fallback if whole-vector tying hurts general text: tie only the top-k principal directions of the entity subspace. (5) Cost per link: one 12-token stop-grad forward plus one 12-token forward/backward. When an alias changes (new manager), the old link is dropped and a tie to the new entity is trained. PRE-GATE (one-off, about 10 min): on the base, patch h_name into the alias position layer by layer on 50 links and measure the rise in hop-2 answer logprob. If hand-patching does not raise two-hop, the tie cannot work, so stop.
candidates.weak_spot: It depends on correct alias -> entity links (the tagger catches 67% of mentions). A wrong tie wires 'my sister' to another person's facts, giving a confident wrong join, which is worse than abstaining. Pulling the residual stream could distort generic text that contains the alias word ('sister' in general), and the KL anchor may not fully catch this. Cosine-tying a whole residual vector may be too blunt.
candidates.why_new: BRACE (NeurIPS 2026, forum dPo7MFIbmu) diagnoses the same bridge-entity mismatch but fixes it by rewriting training text with a shared descriptor pool (a data method). 'Hopping too late' (2406.12775) is analysis plus inference-time back-patching, not training. Identity Bridge (2602.02470) adds identity-style data. In the project, bridge dreams, b4_bridge and the queued graph-walk and uncovered-pairs-first ideas all add generated co-context text, so they scale with pairs dreamed. ASTie trains a hidden-state alignment target taken from the model's own name-position state inside the KL-anchored nightly LoRA. It scales with entities (N), not pairs (N^2), and is cross-day by construction: facts learned before the link was formed become joinable. No queued or tried item ties representations.
candidates.k2_test: DATA (new; Claude Batches): extend the Week-2 fact world with about 60 bridge entities, each with an alias stated on day d1 and 2-4 attribute facts stated on other days. Two-hop questions are split into DREAMED (pairs the b4_nb dreamer covered) and NEVER-CO-OCCURRED (checked by grep: no training sequence, dream or names item holds both alias and attribute). Exact match after NFKC. PRE-GATE: hand-patching the name state at the best layer must raise the base's never-co-occurred hop-2 accuracy by >= 10 points, or the arms are not run. ARMS (one change): A = ab_ob_b4_nb; B = A + L_tie; EQUAL-COMPUTE C = A with the tie's extra FLOPs spent on extra bridge dreams plus a names re-read (same wall-clock and tokens, measured). Fair comparison B vs C. 2 seeds, paired McNemar per item (paired.py). PASS (PREREG): never-co-occurred two-hop B >= C + 12 (p<0.05 both seeds); one-hop recall within 2 of C; ARC within 1; diary reading within 2 of C; wrong-person join rate not above C. WRONG IF: never-co-occurred gain < 4 while the tie converges (cos > 0.9). That means aligned states do not cause joins on K2.
candidates.mac_fit: SERVE: zero cost. Same LoRA, no extra tokens, no tok/s change on the M1 Pro or the 8 GB M2. NIGHT: about 100-300 links a night add about 3-8% to a b4 night. Peak memory unchanged (strings are shorter than the 256-token dream micro-batches), so it fits the 5 GB cap on the 8 GB M2.
candidates.test_cost: Kaggle T4x2: pre-gate about 0.5 GPU-h; 3 arms x 2 seeds of a 7-night Week-2 run at about 1.2 h each = about 7-8 GPU-h (the 5070 Ti can take one seed). Claude Batches for world, paraphrases and grading: about $1.5-2.5.

closest_work.overlap: Bridge resolved in early layers, second hop too late; back-patching fixes up to 66% of errors. Analysis plus inference-time patching only, no training. Supports the PRE-GATE idea of patching the name state at a chosen layer.

closest_work.title: Why Knowing Both Hops Is Not Enough: Understanding Two-Hop Generalization in Language Models (Zhang et al., Aug 2026)
closest_work.overlap: Attributes two-hop success to consistent intermediate representations of the same entity across contexts and failure to a cross-layer mismatch. Trains from scratch in a symbolic setting with a recurrent strategy; no alignment or tying loss; no fine-tuned-knowledge experiments. Supports the mechanism, not the method. New to the project.

closest_work.title: Two-hop curse (Balesni, Korbak, Evans)
closest_work.overlap: Latent two-hop fails when facts sit in different documents. This is the baseline failure ASTie targets; it does not propose representation tying.

prior.notes: Verdict: partly-new. No paper found that trains an explicit residual-level cosine/MSE tie between an alias-position state and the entity-name-position state inside a nightly LoRA with a KL anchor. Searches (about 6 web searches, 2 fetches) found nothing matching the alias-to-entity tie or the 'alias -> name state' LoRA loss, and no 'alias' or 'tying' representation objective for two-hop. The mechanism's core observation (bridge representation alignment drives two-hop) is already reported by Identity Bridge (2509.24653) and DiscoLoop (2607.00341), and BRACE (NeurIPS 2026, dPo7MFIbmu) fixes the same mismatch with data. So the 'why_new' claim that no queued or tried item ties representations is supported by this search, but the proposal should cite Identity Bridge as the closest mechanistic precedent and note its alignment-tracks-generalization finding. Two corrections to the proposal text: (1) the proposal cites Identity Bridge as 2602.02470; the id for Identity Bridge is 2509.24653. 2602.02470 is a separate 'Identity Bridge reversal' paper per raw/02-batch-a.md line 24, so the citation should be checked. (2) 2509.24653 is in known-ids (line 664) but raw/02-batch-a.md tags it NEW, so the project's sweep notes are inconsistent. Other ids seen in search and NOT in known-ids: 2608.07261, 2502.10835 (Back Attention, multi-hop, architectural), 2601.03542 (Layer-Order Inversion: final-answer entity decodable earlier than bridge in some layers, a counterexample to a strict hop-ordering assumption relevant to choosing La..Lb), 2502.13913 (two-hop in context). Also 2604.03384 not known and not checked for content. Risks for the proposal: the layer-order-inversion result (2601.03542) suggests the layer window (25-45% depth) and the 'bridge resolved first' assumption may not hold on all models; the tie target may not be where the bridge is resolved. The PRE-GATE is still the right first check. Limits: BRACE's arXiv id is unknown, so the known-ids grep could not be run for it. The NeurIPS page fetch gave the forum id match, but it is a single-source reading.

fatal_flaws: The pre-gate as written cannot pass. It patches h_name into the alias position on the BASE model, but the base has never learned Maya's attributes, so hop-2 accuracy stays near 0 whatever is patched. The gate has to run on an arm-A checkpoint that already answers one-hop by name ('Maya's phone number is'). As written it will either stop a good idea or get waved through. (shown by the logic of the design)

The N-vs-N^2 argument is wrong for this kind of join, and the result is a cheaper data baseline that the test leaves out. An alias join needs (alias x that entity's attributes) items, which grows linearly with facts, not with entity pairs. For each confirmed link you can rewrite every stored fact about Maya with 'Ben's sister' in her place: a deterministic string swap with no Claude cost and no hidden-state hooks. Arm C (extra bridge dreams plus a names re-read) is the wrong rival. Without an alias-substitution arm, a B > C win says nothing about whether tying states beats the obvious data fix. (suggested: substitution is the same family as BRACE's shared descriptors, which BRACE reports works)

For real assistant use there is a near-free serve-time rival the proposal ignores. The tagger already produces an (alias -> entity) table, so you can put a line like 'Ben's sister = Maya' in the system prompt or rewrite the query before decoding. Then hop 1 sits in context, and the two-hop curse (Balesni et al.) applies only to latent joins of two facts both held in weights. This rival also updates the instant a link changes (new manager) and is checkable, whereas a weight tie keeps its error until it is untrained. Unless ASTie beats it on a task where the table cannot be used, the real-use case is weak. (suggested, untested on K2)
fixable_flaws: The WRONG-IF criterion 'cos > 0.9' carries no information. Raw residual vectors in mid layers are dominated by a few massive-activation dimensions and a shared mean direction, so cosine between any two entity states is often already above 0.9 on the base model. Compute the tie and its convergence check on states with the mean removed and outlier dimensions masked (or whitened with dev-set statistics). Report the base-model value of the same metric so 'converged' means something. (suggested; check on K2 in 5 minutes)

Choose the tie position and layers with the trained A checkpoint, not the base. Facts written by the nightly LoRA can be read out at different depths than pretraining facts, and Layer-Order Inversion (2601.03542) warns that a 'bridge resolved first' layer window may not hold. Scan every layer at both the last alias token ('sister') and the possessive token, and fix La..Lb before any arm runs. (untested)

Changing a link is not handled. Dropping the old link from the loss does not undo a tie already in the weights, so 'Ben's manager' keeps pointing at the old manager. You need an explicit untie, for example a margin loss pushing the alias state away from the old name state, and a test item for it (a link changes on day 5, query on day 7). (suggested)

Collateral damage is under-tested. ARC and diary reading will not catch 'Maya's sister' or 'Tom's sister' drifting toward Maya. Add probes for the same alias word with a different owner and for the reverse direction ('Maya's brother' -> Ben), and require one-hop accuracy on them within 2 points of A. (untested)

Bad links are only described, never measured. Run one arm with 15% of links deliberately mis-assigned, at the tagger's real error rate, and measure the confident wrong-join rate against abstention. That is the failure Ben would actually see. (untested)

Citation fix, already flagged: Identity Bridge is 2509.24653, not 2602.02470. Also cite RippleEdits-style alias tests from knowledge editing, and ROME/MEMIT's finding that facts are keyed at the last subject token in mid-layer MLPs. ASTie is in effect 'give the alias the same key', which narrows the novelty claim to the training-loss form inside a KL-anchored nightly LoRA. (shown by the prior-art check plus known literature)

The big Qwen3.6-35B-A3B backbone has Gated DeltaNet layers, and their recurrent state behaves differently from attention residuals at the alias position. Keep every claim to K2-3.7B until it is tested separately. (untested)
attack.fair_baseline: Two baselines, both matched on night tokens and wall-clock. (1) C_sub: A plus deterministic alias-substitution augmentation. For each confirmed link, every stored attribute fact about the entity is rewritten with the alias in place of the name ('Ben's sister's phone number is ...'), spending the tie's extra FLOPs on these sentences. This is the BRACE-style data fix in its cheapest form. (2) D_serve: A with no training change, plus the tagger's alias table injected at serve time (one system-prompt line per link mentioned in the query, or a query rewrite). D_serve is the real-use rival. C_sub is the fair equal-compute training rival. Arm C as proposed (extra bridge dreams plus a names re-read) is a weaker rival and can stay as a third comparison.
attack.likely_effect: Against the proposed arm C (bridge dreams): maybe +5 to +15 points on never-co-occurred alias joins, if the pre-gate (run correctly on an A checkpoint) shows patching helps. That is suggested by back-patching fixing up to 66% of errors in Hopping Too Late, and untested on K2 or on LoRA-written facts. Against C_sub (substitution augmentation): about 0, possibly worse, because substitution trains the exact query form (suggested). Against D_serve (in-context alias line): likely worse on accuracy and much worse on handling changed links (suggested). The one place ASTie could win outright is cross-day joins where the old fact text is no longer kept, so substitution has nothing to rewrite and the alias table is unavailable at serve time. That case is untested and may not exist in Ben's setup, where logs and the names pass are kept. Net real-use effect: small (untested).
attack.improved_test: SMALL K2-3.7B CARD WORLD ONLY (keep it separate from the village model). DATA (Claude Batches, about $2): extend the Week-2 fact world with 60 bridge entities. Each gets an alias stated on day d1 and 3 attributes stated on other days, giving 180 hop-2 items. For 20 of the entities, the attributes come in week 1 and the link only in week 2, and week-1 raw text is removed from all rewrite sources. This is the cross-day split. Splits: never-co-occurred (checked by grep over every training sequence, dream and names item), dreamed, cross-day, link-changed (10 links reassigned on day 5), and collateral probes (the same alias word with a different owner, and reverse direction). Scoring is exact match after NFKC; wrong-person answers are counted separately from abstentions. PRE-GATE (on the A checkpoint after 7 nights, not the base): patch name states into the alias position, using mean-removed states with outliers masked, at each layer and at both candidate token positions, on 50 dev links. Fix the best window in advance. Gate: hop-2 accuracy on never-co-occurred items rises by at least 15 points at some window, otherwise stop. Also record the base-model cosine between unrelated entities with the same metric. ARMS (one change each, 2 seeds, same 7 nights, night tokens and wall-clock measured and matched within 5%): A = ab_ob_b4_nb; B = A + L_tie (lambda 0.3, fixed on a dev world beforehand); C_sub = A + alias-substitution augmentation filling the tie's compute budget; C_dream = A + extra bridge dreams (the original C); D_serve = A + serve-time alias line (no training change; reported, not compute-matched); B_noisy = B with 15% of links mis-assigned. STATS: paired McNemar per item (paired.py), each seed separately. PASS (fixed in advance): never-co-occurred hop-2 B >= C_sub + 8 and >= C_dream + 12, p < 0.05 on both seeds; cross-day B >= C_sub + 10; one-hop within 2 of A; collateral probes within 2 of A; ARC within 1; diary reading within 2; link-changed items: B's old-entity answers no more frequent than C_sub's; B_noisy confident wrong-join rate no more than 1.5x C_sub's under the same noise. To call it useful for the real assistant, B must also come within 5 points of D_serve on never-co-occurred items, or beat it on cross-day items. REFUTED IF: B's gain over C_sub is under 3 points on never-co-occurred items while the centred tie cosine climbs from its base value to within 0.05 of the name-to-name self-cosine. That would mean aligned states do not produce joins on K2. A pre-gate failure also refutes it. COST: about 0.5 GPU-h for the pre-gate plus 6 arms x 2 seeds x about 1.2 h = about 15 GPU-h on Kaggle T4x2. Run the pre-gate first and spend nothing else if it fails. SUMMARY FOR BEN: the idea teaches the model that 'my sister' and 'Maya' should look the same inside its head, so anything it knows about Maya also answers questions about 'my sister'. The catch is that two much simpler tricks probably get the same result: copy Maya's facts with 'my sister' swapped in, or just remind the model 'my sister = Maya' when you ask. The test has to beat those two, not only the weaker version in the plan.

candidates.name: Recall-Then-Read, with nightly key practice (cue-sleep) as stage 2
candidates.one_line: The slept LoRA does one short closed-book pass that names the bridge entities and facts it remembers; those names become extra diary search keys, and the base model with the LoRA switched off reads what comes back. Stage 2 trains the key pass each night, using a free signal: did the query pull up the right diary turn.
candidates.mechanism: SERVE (stage 1, no training): for a question that touches personal memory (gated by the gateway, and only when the FTS5 hit on the raw question is weak): (1) KEY PASS, LoRA ON: a fixed 1-shot prompt asks the slept K2 for up to 4 names and short facts linked to the question ('my sister -> Maya; Maya -> dentist Dr. Lee'), at most 40 tokens, greedy, with per-name mean token logprob logged. (2) RETRIEVE: BM25/FTS5 with queries {question} plus each key, merged by reciprocal-rank fusion and trimmed to the same k_tokens budget as the plain diary baseline (about 1.5k). Keys below logprob tau are dropped. (3) READ PASS, LoRA OFF (the base read the diary best: 84.6 vs 66 for the slept model). The key line can optionally go in as 'hint (may be wrong)'. (4) ABSTAIN HOOK: if no key retrieves a turn that contains it, the gateway says 'not sure, want me to search email/calendar?'. NIGHT (stage 2, only if stage 1 passes): from the day's diary, pick turns holding handles, dates, people or decisions; Claude Batches writes 3 future-style questions per turn, with questions that share rare tokens with the source turn filtered out. The current model samples 8 key-pass outputs per question. Reward = the source turn lands in the top-3 of the real FTS5 index (deterministic, no grader), shortest hit first. SFT on the best hitting key list (one ReST round per night) joins the sleep mix under the same KL anchor. Questions with 0/8 hits become 'cue' targets: a one-line where-to-look sentence ('Priya: scheduling, week of Oct 20, email'), so weights learn where and under what words a memory lives, while the values stay in the diary.
candidates.weak_spot: It adds a serve-time pass (about 40 decode tokens) to memory questions, which competes with the multi-agent tok/s budget. It only helps when one hop is in weights or findable and the other is in the diary; facts never written there gain nothing. Small models misjudge their own confidence (2604.04651), so tau may be badly calibrated; the fallback is always using the keys and letting RRF and the budget absorb noise. The stage-2 reward checks retrieval, not the answer, so a 3.7B reader can still misread a found turn. Toggling the LoRA on mlx needs the adapter unfused, which costs about 5-15% decode speed on the key pass only.
candidates.why_new: IRCoT and self-ask (2212.10509, 2210.03350) form hop-2 queries from retrieved text or the same model's CoT, with no weight memory. HippoRAG uses a text-built KG. Memory-R1 (2508.19828) and Mem-alpha (2509.25911) train memory managers with online RL; 'Search, Do not Guess' (2604.04651) trains always-search on Wikipedia QA. The project's router ('memory if p>=0.5 else diary', 57-60, BAD) chose one source instead of chaining them, and the queued 'search-only-when-unsure' is about WHEN to search, not HOW. New here: the personal-sleep LoRA is used only as a retrieval-key generator, the unslept base does the reading, and (stage 2) the key pass is trained nightly on a free deterministic hit@3 signal from the user's own index, with unrecoverable facts stored as where-to-look cues rather than values.
candidates.k2_test: DATA: Week-2 world with its day-by-day diary (FTS5 of the raw synthetic chats). Add 150 two-hop questions with hop 1 and hop 2 stated on different days (grep-confirmed that no single diary turn holds both), plus the 200 one-hop and 50 never-taught questions. Claude Batches writes and grades (exact match plus NFKC). STAGE 1 ARMS, same ab_ob_b4_nb LoRA seeds 1 and 2, same k_tokens: D0 = base + BM25(question); D1 = slept + BM25(question); EQUAL-COMPUTE D2 = base runs the same 40-token key pass (classic self-ask query expansion, same tokens and passes); R = key pass LoRA ON, read LoRA OFF. PASS (PREREG): cross-day two-hop R >= D2 + 15 and R >= D0 + 20 (paired McNemar p<0.05, both seeds); one-hop R >= D0 - 1; never-taught 'don't know' R >= D0 - 5; added latency per memory question <= 1.5 s on the M1 Pro (K2 q4, measured). WRONG IF: R - D2 < 5 (sleep adds nothing over query expansion). If R two-hop stays < 50 while the key pass names the right bridge on > 80% of items, the read pass cannot join even in one context. STAGE 2 (only if stage 1 passes): R vs R+cue-sleep at equal LoRA steps against open-book rehearsal on the same items; pass hit@3 >= +15 and two-hop >= +8 on held-out days; wrong if hit@3 rises but accuracy stays within 2 (the bottleneck is reading).
candidates.mac_fit: SERVE: K2 q4 2.6 GB plus an unfused r16 LoRA (about 30-60 MB); one model serves both passes, and it fits the 8 GB M2 easily. Extra cost per memory question is about 40 decode tokens at about 36 tok/s (about 1.1 s). The retrieved-text prefill is the same as the plain diary baseline. The Qwen3.6 big tier can use the same code with an adapter toggle. NIGHT: zero for stage 1. Stage 2 is about 200 items x 8 samples x 30 tokens = about 50k generated tokens, about 8-15 min batched on the Mac, plus FTS5 scoring in seconds and about 10% more sleep SFT steps.
candidates.test_cost: Stage 1: no training (reuses ab_ob_b4_nb LoRAs, or about 2.5 T4-h to retrain 2 seeds); inference for 4 arms x 400 questions x 2 seeds is about 1 T4-h; 15 min Mac latency check; Claude Batches about $1-2. Stage 2: about 4.5-5 T4-h per seed (about 10 h for 2), Claude Batches about $3-5.

prior.notes: Verdict: partly-new. The retrieval-key-from-weights idea is well covered by GenRead, Recitation-augmented LM, HyDE and Query2doc. Those are the baselines a reviewer would name, and the proposal's D2 equal-compute arm (base runs the same key pass) is the right control against them. What looks new is the combination: an adapter-on key pass with adapter-off reading, a personal diary as the index, and a nightly stage-2 trained on a deterministic hit@3 reward from the user's own FTS5 index, plus cue-type targets for unrecoverable facts. Known-ids grep results: 2210.03350 (Self-Ask) and 2508.19828 (Memory-R1) and 2503.23895 (Dynamic Parametric RAG) are known. 2212.10509 (IRCoT), 2405.14831 (HippoRAG), 2604.04651 (Search Do not Guess), 2509.25911 (Mem-alpha), 2406.14891 (Generate-then-Ground), 2209.10063 (GenRead), 2212.10496 (HyDE), 2303.07678 (Query2doc), 2210.01296 (Recitation), 2512.20237 (MemR3), 2603.03293 (SE-Search), 2606.04536 are NOT in /mnt/project-files/research/sweep-2026/known-ids.txt. The known-ids file has 1082 lines. Items to fix in the proposal: (a) the 2604.04651 'always search on Wikipedia QA' description is not supported by the search snippets; (b) GenRead, HyDE, Query2doc and Recitation are missing from why_new and should be named as the primary baselines; (c) GenRead, HyDE and Recitation were described from secondary sources only, so their exact claims need primary-text checks. Search budget used: 4 web searches, 0 page fetches.

fatal_flaws: None fatal on their own, but there is one near-fatal problem with the baseline (shown by reading the design). In the proposed K2 test, BOTH hops are written in the diary (on different days). So the right comparison is not 'base writes 40 keys from nothing' (D2). It is ordinary two-round retrieval: retrieve with the question, have the base read the top turns and write the bridge name (sister -> Maya), then retrieve again. That is IRCoT/self-ask with retrieval, or even zero-decode pseudo-relevance feedback (RM3). Another fair arm is a nightly entity/alias table pulled from the diary (sister=Maya, Dr. Lee=dentist) and used for query expansion with no decode at all. As written, D2 is a weak strawman. If R only beats D0 and D2, that does not show the weights add anything a second retrieval round would not. Without these arms the stage-1 result cannot be read.

Stage 2 is not new (suggested, from memory and not checked against primary text). Training a query generator or rewriter on a retrieval-hit reward from a BM25 index is prior work: 'Query Rewriting for Retrieval-Augmented LLMs' (Ma et al. 2023, arXiv 2305.14283) and DeepRetrieval (arXiv 2503.00223, RL on recall/hit reward against real search engines including BM25). The why_new must name these. Then only the 'personal, nightly, plus where-to-look cue targets' part is new.
fixable_flaws: Novelty framing. The serve side is GenRead / Recitation / HyDE / Query2doc / Generate-then-Ground (2406.14891) with a LoRA as the generator. 'Adapter on for keys, adapter off for reading' is a deployment choice, not a mechanism. Rewrite why_new to say so, and remove the unsupported description of 2604.04651 as 'always-search on Wikipedia QA'.

Unverified project number. I could not find the 'base reads diary 84.6 vs slept 66' figure in the repo with a quick grep: the 84.6 hits are unrelated (a dl-7b lost-item premise check, a ROME table, a sleep-smoke time). Point to the exact results file before using it to justify LoRA-off reading.

The test has no condition where weights are the only source of hop 1. Add one: after sleep, delete or garble the diary turn that holds hop 1, so only the LoRA knows 'sister -> Maya'. This is the only case where the mechanism is in principle better than iterative retrieval. Without it, a win could just be a better query-expansion prompt.

Lexical-gap filter. The questions are filtered to share no rare tokens with the source turn. That makes plain BM25 look artificially bad and inflates every expansion arm. Report results on both the filtered set and an unfiltered or naturally phrased set, ideally with about 50 questions Ben writes himself about a real or synthetic week.

Multi-agent cost is understated. On mlx-lm, a per-request adapter toggle generally breaks shared batched decode with other agents (mixed-adapter batching is not standard; untested here). The read pass also cannot reuse the key pass's KV/prompt cache, because the weights differ, so the question and system prompt are prefilled twice. On Qwen3.6 the Gated DeltaNet recurrent state likewise cannot be shared. Measure the tok/s of the OTHER agents while key passes run, not just the 1.1 s on the memory question.
Calibration of tau. Preregister tau=-inf (always use keys) as the main arm and treat the logprob gate as a secondary ablation. Otherwise tau gets tuned on the test set.

Stage-2 reward drift. hit@3 is measured against today's index, and the index grows every night, so a key list that hits today may miss in a month. Also, a model that 'learns distinctive tokens of a turn' is really memorizing diary content, which overlaps with ordinary sleep. Score stage 2 on held-out days AND against a later, larger index (for example day 14 against the full 14-day index).

Stage 2 compares against 'open-book rehearsal' but leaves out the obvious cheaper alternative: the same nightly Claude Batches budget used to build the alias/entity table (D4), which needs no training at all.
attack.fair_baseline: Equal decode budget (40 tokens, one extra retrieval round): base model, LoRA off. Round 1 runs BM25 on the question, the base reads the top-k turns and writes up to 4 bridge names/facts in 40 tokens (self-ask/IRCoT-lite over the diary), round 2 runs BM25 on question+keys, merged with RRF, trimmed to the same 1.5k k_tokens, and the base reads. A second zero-decode baseline: a nightly alias/entity table (relation triples pulled from the day's diary by Claude Batches or the base) used for deterministic query expansion. I expect one of these two to match R on cross-day two-hop whenever both hops are in the diary.
attack.likely_effect: Suggested (by reasoning, nothing run): on the proposed lexical-gap-filtered cross-day two-hop set, R likely beats D0 (question-only BM25) by a lot, +15 to +30 points, because D0 often cannot find hop 2 at all. Against the base key pass D2, R probably wins by +5 to +15 when the slept LoRA really holds 'sister -> Maya' (the 91% one-hop recall from weights supports this, though that 91% was measured on names, not relations). Against a fair two-round retrieval or alias-table baseline, my guess is +0 to +5 when both hops are in the diary, and +10 or more only in the condition where hop 1 lives in weights alone. Untested: the size of the real-use gain. Cross-day personal two-hop questions are probably a small share of Ben's real requests, and many are answered by email/calendar tool search. So the net assistant-level effect is likely small, low single digits on a mixed real-task suite. Stage 2's gain over stage 1 is untested. My guess is +5 to +10 hit@3 on held-out days, which may fade as the index grows.
attack.improved_test: DATA. Week-2 world, FTS5 over the raw diary. 150 cross-day two-hop items (grep-confirmed that no single turn holds both hops), 200 one-hop items, 50 never-taught items. Two phrasings of every two-hop item: (a) lexical-gap-filtered, (b) natural (Claude writes it as Ben would, no filter), plus 50 items Ben writes himself. Condition W ('weights-only hop 1'): for 75 of the two-hop items, remove the hop-1 turn from the index after sleep, so the bridge exists only in the LoRA. Grading is exact match + NFKC via Claude Batches. Also log bridge-named-correctly and hit@3 for each hop, so the failure stage is visible. ARMS (same ab_ob_b4_nb LoRA, seeds 1 and 2, same 1.5k k_tokens, same reader = base LoRA-off unless stated): D0 = BM25(question). D1 = slept reader + BM25(question). D2 = base writes a 40-token closed-book key pass. D3 = two-round retrieval: base reads the round-1 hits and writes 40-token bridge keys, then round 2 (equal decode). D4 = nightly alias/entity table expansion (zero decode; table built by Claude Batches from the same diary). R = slept LoRA-on key pass, LoRA-off read. R+D3 = slept keys added to round 2 (tells whether the two are complementary). Main arm uses tau = -inf; the tau gate is an ablation. PASS MARKS (fixed before running): on natural-phrasing cross-day two-hop, R >= max(D3, D4) + 8 on both seeds (paired McNemar p<0.05 pooled). On condition W, R >= max(D3, D4) + 15. One-hop R >= D0 - 1. Never-taught 'don't know' R >= D0 - 5. Added wall-clock per memory question <= 1.5 s on the M1 Pro (K2 q4, including the second prefill). With 3 other agents decoding at the same time, their tok/s drop is <= 10% while key passes run. RESULT THAT REFUTES IT: R - max(D3, D4) < 3 on natural phrasing AND < 8 on condition W. Then sleep-as-key-generator adds nothing over a second retrieval round or a cheap alias table, and the idea is dropped, stage 2 included. DIAGNOSTIC: if R names the right bridge on > 80% of items but two-hop accuracy stays < 50, the bottleneck is the reader. In that case stop and work on reading, not keys. STAGE 2 (only if stage 1 passes): R+cue-sleep vs R vs R+D4-table-refreshed-nightly, at equal nightly Claude spend and equal LoRA steps. Score on held-out days 8-14 against the full growing index. Pass if hit@3 >= +10 and two-hop accuracy >= +6 over the better of R and R+D4. Refuted if hit@3 rises but accuracy moves < 2, or if the gain at the day-14 index is under half the day-8 gain.

candidates.name: Tripwire lines (learned pre-mortem cues fired by the model at the trap state)
candidates.one_line: Each night, every mistake becomes a short self-warning that the model learns to write for itself just before the step where it went wrong, and to write at the same kind of state in good runs too. Later it writes the warning when it reaches a similar state, then acts on it.
candidates.mechanism: DAY: the gateway logs every agent run. A run is a mistake if a tool returns an error, the user corrects the agent in the next turn, the tau2 reward is 0, or a batched Claude grader marks it failed. NIGHT step 1 (Claude Batches, Sonnet): for each failed run, find the first wrong step t and write (a) a tripwire of at most 15 tokens in a fixed <tw>...</tw> tag on the scratch channel that names the trap, not the answer ('<tw>two order ids given; confirm which before refund</tw>'), (b) the corrected action at t, and (c) a trap type from a growing per-user list of about 5-30 types. Step 2: Claude marks states of the same trap types in the day's GOOD runs. Step 3: LoRA data of three kinds. Fire-on-failure: prefix to t -> tripwire + corrected action. Fire-on-success: prefix to the marked good state -> tripwire + the action taken, so the line keys on the state, not on failure. No-fire: ordinary good steps with no tripwire, which teaches restraint. All of this joins the skill-sleep LoRA mix (same KL anchor on 100 general prompts, same rank). SERVE: the model emits tripwires on its own; the gateway keeps them in context so the next action is conditioned on them. A tripwire that fired before a run that still failed is upweighted the next night. A trap type that fired and failed on 3 nights becomes an ask-tripwire ('<tw>unsure which account; ask</tw>' + a question).
candidates.weak_spot: (1) The model may write the tripwire and then ignore it, so the line is decoration; at 3.7B the link between line and action may be weak. (2) Claude's first-wrong-step and trap types may be wrong or too narrow, so lines do not carry to new tasks. (3) It may fire too often, costing tokens and asking annoying questions; the no-fire examples and a fire-rate pass mark are there to catch this.
candidates.why_new: ERL (2603.24639) and ReMe (2512.10696) keep heuristics in the prompt, which costs tokens and needs retrieval. 2509.20562 uses a separate model that reflects after a failure. Divergence-point DPO (2606.23112) and Agent-R (2501.11425) train only the corrected action, with no stated reason. AgentHER (2603.21357) relabels goals. Project Skill-Sleep A2 is SFT/DPO/KTO on whole runs with no cue. New: the lesson goes into weights as a line the model writes itself at the state where it is needed, before acting; it is trained to fire on good runs of the same trap type; and fired-then-failed tripwires feed the next night and turn into ask-tripwires.
candidates.k2_test: tau2 retail, K2-3.7B bf16 (q4 fake-quant eval at the end), no-think. Split by task id into about 74 train tasks and 40 held-out tasks never seen at night. Collect 3 trials per train task (about 222 runs, Haiku 5.5 user sim); label with Sonnet through Batches. ARMS, one night each on the same runs, same rank, KL anchor, optimizer steps and trained tokens: B = base; C0 = correction SFT on the same examples with target = corrected action only (equal-compute baseline, padded with replay to match tokens); T = tripwire data. Eval: 40 held-out tasks x 4 trials, pass^1, paired by task-trial McNemar (paired.py). PASS (PREREG): T >= C0 + 8/160 (p<0.05); held-out fire rate 0.3-3 per task; general-prompt KL and ARC within 1 of C0. Diagnostic: >= 40% of held-out firings are on steps a blind Claude grader calls real traps. REFUTED if T <= C0 + 2/160, or held-out tripwires fire but the next action is no more often correct than C0's at the same steps (decoration). Second seed only if the first passes. Collection runs and labels are shared with the Error-and-provenance gate candidate.
candidates.mac_fit: SERVE: no extra memory beyond the planned adapter (q4 K2 about 2.6 GB + tens of MB). About 15 tokens per fired tripwire; at 1-2 fires per task and 30+ tok/s that is about 0.5-1 s per task, and the line can be shown to Ben as a 'watching for...' hint. Same on the 8 GB M2. NIGHT: tripwires add at most about 15 tokens to sequences skill-sleep already trains on (within about 5% of the A2 recipe). Labeling runs in the cloud through Batches, so the Mac does no extra work.
candidates.test_cost: About 222 collection runs + 3 arms x 160 eval runs on K2 fp16 vLLM on Kaggle T4x2, about 6-8 T4-h; LoRA nights about 1.5 h. About 8-10 of the weekly 30 h, or the 5070 Ti when free. Claude: Haiku 5.5 user sim for about 700 runs, about $8-12; Sonnet labeling through Batches, about $3-5. About $11-17 in all, less when collection is shared.
