prior.notes:
Verdict: partly-new. Pieces exist separately: corrected-action SFT at the failure step (LEAFE 2603.16843, Agent-R/divergence-point work), privileged hint or reflection distilled into weights (LEAFE, AHEAD 2608.24114), model-written reflections trained by SFT (Agent-Reflex 2610.17953, SRFT 2610.04269). I found no paper where the model learns to emit a short trap-named cue at the state, trains it with fire-on-success and no-fire negatives, and tracks fire rate and fired-then-failed escalation. The proposal's novel part is the cue plus the fire-on-good-runs and no-fire training, not the corrected-action training.

Known-ids check (grep -c on /mnt/project-files/research/sweep-2026/known-ids.txt): only 2512.10696 and 2603.21357 hit. These checked as 0 (not known): 2603.24639, 2509.20562, 2606.23112, 2603.16843, 2504.13145, 2610.04269, 2610.17953, 2601.01580, 2606.04536, 2610.27495, 2607.27937, 2606.31270, 2608.24114, 2608.11772, 2607.27443, 2601.22132, 2608.18884, 2410.06638, 2605.27690, 2608.24777, 2509.26354. 2501.11425 (Agent-R) was grep-checked as 0 but I did not read its paper. The known-ids file holds bare ids, so grep for hint/tripwire/warning/cue finds nothing.

Risks to flag: 2601.01580 reports that plain SFT on reflection data did not raise self-correction rate, which is direct evidence for weak_spot (1). LEAFE is the strongest comparator; C0 is essentially LEAFE-style training, so the pre-registered T vs C0 test is the real novelty check. AHEAD's hints are teacher-side (privileged), which differs from the proposal's policy-emitted tripwire. Only abstracts or snippets were read for 2608.24114, 2610.17953, and 2603.16843, so their details should be verified against full text before citing. Searches used: 5 of 8; page fetches used: 1 of 4."

fatal_flaws: None fatal to the idea itself. The planned K2 test is fatal as a novelty test: C0 is the wrong baseline. T gets three things C0 lacks: (i) a written reason before the action, (ii) extra supervised good-run states (fire-on-success), (iii) no-fire restraint examples. Padding C0 'with replay to match tokens' matches token count, not supervised decision states. If T beats C0, nobody can say whether the gain came from the cue, from rationale-style SFT (already done in Agent-Reflex 2610.17953 / LEAFE 2603.16843, suggested from snippets), or from more good-state data. Without the arms listed under improved_test, a pass would not show anything new.

The cheapest competitor is missing. The why_new argument against prompt-held heuristics (ERL/ReMe 'cost tokens and need retrieval') does not hold at this scale. The proposal caps the per-user list at about 5-30 trap types of 15 tokens each, so the whole list is about 450 tokens. That fits in a prefix-cached system prompt and needs no retrieval (shown by arithmetic). A zero-training arm P (C0 or base plus the trap list in the system prompt) must be beaten, or the weight-based cue has no real-use case. The one exception is if prompt adherence at 3.7B is the bottleneck, which is untested.
fixable_flaws: Statistics. McNemar on 160 task-trial pairs treats the 4 trials of a task as independent, but tau2 trials within a task are strongly correlated, so p is too optimistic. Use a paired bootstrap clustered by task (resample the 40 tasks), or McNemar on per-task majority outcomes. As written, +8/160 is about 5 pp. With clustering, that is likely underpowered at 40 tasks (suggested). Raise eval to 40 tasks x 8 trials, or add airline as a second held-out domain.

The decoration check compares T's next action with C0's 'at the same steps'. Held-out runs diverge, so the same steps mostly do not exist. Replace it with an intervention on T's own runs: at each held-out firing, (a) delete the tw line, (b) swap in a tw line from a different trap type, (c) keep it, and resample the next action from the same prefix 8 times each. If the line matters, the action changes and correctness drops under (a) and (b).

Escalation (fired-then-failed upweighting, ask-tripwires after 3 nights) cannot be exercised in a one-night test, yet it is listed as part of the novelty. Either drop it from this claim or add a 3-night sequential arm later. Also, the tau2 user sim answers questions, so ask-tripwires will look free there but cost Ben patience in real use.

Label noise. A 0 reward on tau2 retail often comes from capability failures (wrong arithmetic, wrong tool args, policy misread), not from a nameable trap. Sonnet will still invent a trap and a first-wrong-step. Add a step where Sonnet labels 'no nameable trap' and drops the run, and have a second grader re-label 30 runs to measure agreement on step t and trap type. If agreement on t is below 60%, the data is mostly noise.

Base-rate risk. K2-3.7B no-think pass^1 on retail is probably low (suggested about 15-30%). Most failures may be beyond what a 15-token cue can fix, which caps the gain. Measure B first and report the share of failures Sonnet calls trap-type.

Fire-on-success labels come from Claude marking states 'of the same trap type' in good runs. That is a second noisy labeler, and it can teach the model to fire on almost any refund or exchange step. Log the train-set fire rate per trap type and cap the number of fire-on-success examples per type.

Real-use data volume. Ben's day may produce only 0-5 real mistakes, so one night has far less data than 222 tau2 runs. The test should also report a 20-failure subsample arm, which is what one real night looks like.
attack.fair_baseline: C0+ (equal compute): SFT on exactly the same supervised decision states as T, meaning the corrected action at t for failures, the taken action at the marked good states, and the same ordinary no-fire good steps, with no tw line. Match optimizer steps and states, and let T's roughly 15 extra tokens per state be the only difference. Alongside it run R: the same states, but the target is a free-form Claude rationale of about 15 tokens plus the action (Agent-Reflex/LEAFE style), only at failure steps. Run P: C0+ plus the trap-type list (about 450 tokens) in the system prompt. My guess is that P or C0+ matches T. R would match T if the cue's value is just 'think before acting'.
attack.likely_effect: Untested. My guess on tau2 retail held-out tasks: T over C0+ by 0-4 pp pass^1, which would not clear +8/160 once trials are clustered by task. T over the original C0 might reach 3-7 pp, mostly from the extra good-state data and the rationale effect, not from the cue (suggested). 2601.01580's finding that plain SFT on reflection text does not raise self-correction points the same way (suggested, abstract-level). Fire-rate control within 0.3-3 per task is likely achievable with no-fire data (suggested). In real assistant use, the main shown-to-user value is the readable 'watching for...' hint. That is interpretability and trust, not accuracy, and the prompt-list baseline P gives most of it too.
attack.improved_test: DATA: tau2 retail. Split by task id into 74 train and 40 held-out tasks, and add tau2 airline held-out (about 20 tasks) as a transfer check. Collect 3 trials per train task with the Haiku 5.5 user sim, shared with the provenance-gate candidate. Sonnet labels each run through Batches with a 'no nameable trap' option. A second Sonnet pass re-labels 30 runs. Precondition, fixed in advance: agreement on first-wrong-step t of at least 60%, else stop and fix labels first. ARMS: one night each, from the same base, same rank, same KL anchor, same optimizer steps, same set of supervised decision states. B = base. C0+ = all of T's states (failure t, marked good states, no-fire steps) with action-only targets. R = failure states only, target = Claude free rationale (15 tokens or fewer) plus the corrected action. P = C0+ weights plus the trap-type list in the system prompt. T = full tripwire data. T-gen = T with every tw text replaced by a generic '<tw>check details before acting</tw>' (same tokens, no trap content). EVAL: 40 retail held-out tasks x 8 trials (320 runs per arm) plus airline 20 x 4, q4 fake-quant, no-think. Primary statistic: paired difference in pass^1, with a 95% CI from a bootstrap that resamples tasks. PASS MARKS (prereg): T minus max(C0+, P, R) at least +5 pp with the lower CI bound above 0; T minus T-gen at least +3 pp (the trap content matters, not just a pause); held-out fire rate 0.3-3 per task; KL on 100 general prompts and ARC within 1 point of C0+; airline no worse than C0+ by more than 2 pp. CAUSAL CHECK: on T's held-out runs, at every firing step resample the next action 8 times with the tw line kept, deleted, or swapped for another trap type. PASS if correctness with the line kept beats deletion by at least 10 pp and swapping changes the action distribution (total variation 0.15 or more). REFUTED if T is within 2 pp of max(C0+, P, R), if T is within 1 pp of T-gen, or if deleting the line changes next-action correctness by less than 3 pp (decoration). Second seed and the 3-night escalation arm run only if the primary passes. Cost: about 6 arms x 400 runs is about 2,400 eval runs, roughly 2.5x the original. Spread it over 2 Kaggle weeks or use the 5070 Ti. Haiku user-sim cost rises to about $25-35.

candidates.name: Error-and-provenance gate (nightly per-user error probe plus argument-source check before risky calls)
candidates.one_line: Before an irreversible tool call, the gateway checks where each key argument came from (request, context, deterministic resolver, diary, or nowhere), and a tiny linear probe on K2's hidden state, retrained each night on Ben's real corrections, scores how likely the call is one of the model's usual mistakes. If the gate fires, the agent redrafts the call or asks a one-tap question built from its own runner-up value.
candidates.mechanism: SERVE (gateway plus a custom mlx-lm step; no policy change): tools are tagged reversible or irreversible (send_email, delete_file, create/accept event, payments, git push). (1) PROVENANCE: for each argument of a call (recipients, ids, dates, paths; bodies and subjects are exempt), label it grounded (exact or NFKC-fuzzy match in context), resolved (deterministic resolver: relative date -> absolute, nickname -> address via contacts), diary (BM25 hit), or orphan. (2) PROBE: at the call's closing token, read the residual vector from 2-3 middle layers (about 12 KB per call; already computed during decoding) and compute p = probe(h), about 3k multiply-adds per layer. (3) GATE: an orphan argument on an irreversible call, or p above a cost-scaled threshold, fires the gate. Then fork from the cached KV prefix (plain-attention K2 is trimmable), sample 2 more candidate calls at T=0.7, and score each by the probe at its own closing token. If the best candidate is below tau and fully grounded, run it. Otherwise (or if the call is irreversible and any argument is orphan), ask: 'Send to A (x@..) or B (y@..)?', where A is the emitted value, B is the runner-up from re-scoring the argument span over top-k first-token alternatives, plus 'something else'. Reversible calls with no orphan are never gated. NIGHT: (1) after the sleep LoRA trains, recompute h on the day's logged calls plus a rolling 14-day replay with the NEW adapter (old features go stale). (2) Fit a logistic probe per layer plus a per-trap-type bias, L2 and class balancing, in seconds on CPU; calibrate tau on a held-out slice to a target fire rate of about 10%. Labels: tool error, user correction or undo in the next turns, env diff, or a Claude Batches verdict. Before real data exists, start from synthetic labels where Claude removed an argument's source. Ben's answers to gate questions go into the diary, so next time the value is diary-grounded and the gate stays quiet. Each successful redraft gives a free (first draft rejected, redraft chosen) DPO pair for skill-sleep.
candidates.weak_spot: Some legitimate values are inferred and match nothing ('email the guy from yesterday's call'), so they will be flagged orphan and cause extra questions unless the resolver list and exemptions are tuned. If K2's errors are policy errors rather than noisy draws, all 3 drafts share the mistake and the gain must come from asking, which tau2 only rewards if the simulated user answers usefully. Few real labels per day (about 5-30), so the probe can overfit or just track surface features ('refund calls are risky'); the type-prior baseline tests for that. The runner-up value may be junk when the model has no real second guess. Probe quality can drop after each night's weight change, which is handled by refitting on recomputed features.
candidates.why_new: SAPLMA and ITI probes detect false QA statements and are trained once offline; process reward models are large, separate and offline. 'Search, Do not Guess' (2604.04651) shows a small model's own confidence is a poor gate; here the main gate is an external argument-source check, and the probe is fit to this model's own past real errors. AgentAbstain (2607.10059) is only a benchmark; SAGE-Agent (2511.08798) uses a hand-built EVPI model; ActionRating (2606.11349) learns clarify as an action. The project's Dopamine d_value (ruled out) trained the policy; this never trains the policy. New: a per-argument provenance check on irreversible calls only, plus a per-user error probe retrained nightly on features recomputed after each sleep update, used to gate cheap local redrafts and one-tap runner-up questions, and to mine DPO pairs for sleep.
candidates.k2_test: Two sets, same K2-3.7B weights (no sleep LoRA, to isolate the gate). (a) tau2 retail: the same 74/40 split and 222 collection runs as the Tripwire candidate; label each write/lookup call wrong if not in the gold action set or the env diff shows harm. Eval 40 held-out tasks x 4 trials. (b) ARGUMENT-GAP SET (Claude Batches): 400 email/calendar/files/git tasks with mock MCP tools and 3-8k contexts, 200 complete and 200 with one irreversible-call argument removed or made ambiguous (two contacts named Sam, 'the doc' with 3 matches); 100 dev / 300 test, thresholds tuned on dev only. ARMS, matched fire rate (10% on train calls) and the same k=3 redraft budget: G0 = no gate (prompt 'ask if any required detail is missing'); GE = entropy gate with highest-logprob redraft; GV = verbalized-confidence gate (same-compute self-assessment); GT = trap-type prior gate (surface rule); GP = provenance + probe gate. PASS (PREREG): probe held-out AUROC >= 0.72 and >= GT + 0.05; tau2 GP pass^1 >= GE + 6/160 and >= GT + 4/160 (McNemar p<0.05); argument-gap paired accuracy GP >= max(GE, GV) + 15; GP wrong-irreversible rate <= half of GV's; over-asking on complete tasks <= GV + 3; ask rate <= 1 per 3 tau2 tasks. REFUTED if AUROC < 0.65, GP <= GE + 2/160 on tau2, or the argument-gap gain comes only from over-asking (complete-task accuracy drops > 5). Report a probe lesion (provenance rules only). Follow-up if it passes: 3 simulated nights with feature refit; AUROC drop <= 0.05.
candidates.mac_fit: SERVE: probe weights about 40 KB; provenance matching is CPU string/FTS5 work in ms. Needs a small mlx_lm.server patch to expose one hidden state per call (fallback: top-k logprobs at argument tokens). Redrafts fire on about 10% of calls, about 40 tokens from a shared prefix, about 0.3 s per call on average; questions only on gated irreversible calls. Same on the 8 GB M2. On the Qwen3.6 big tier the provenance rules work as-is, but redraft forking needs a DeltaNet state snapshot (unbuilt), so start on K2. NIGHT: one prefill pass over the day's calls (minutes) plus a CPU fit (seconds); under 5% of the night budget; about 12 KB stored per call.
candidates.test_cost: tau2 arms: about 6-8 T4-h with a custom HF loop and hidden-state hook (collection shared with Tripwire). Argument-gap set: about 3-4 T4-h plus 0.5 h hidden-state dump. Total about 10-12 T4-h. Claude: Haiku user sim for 640 eval runs about $7-10; task writing and grading about $3-5 (Sonnet spot-check on 100 for grader trust, kappa plus position swap). About $10-15.

fatal_flaws: The argument-gap set decides the result before the test runs (shown, by reading the design). Its 200 'gap' tasks are made by deleting or blurring an argument's source. Provenance checking is built to catch exactly that, so GP beating GE/GV by 15 points there would only show that the generator and the detector match. It says nothing about K2's real mistakes. As written, the headline pass mark cannot fail for the right reason.

On tau2 retail the gate mostly targets the wrong kind of error (suggested). In retail, nearly every write argument (order id, item id, payment id) is copied from the user or from an earlier lookup result, so provenance will label almost all of them grounded. K2's typical failures there are policy and choice errors: the wrong item among grounded options, exchange when it should be return, acting when the policy forbids it. Grounded-but-wrong calls pass the provenance check, so all the tau2 gain has to come from the probe. That makes the tau2 arm mainly a test of 2608.27750-style probing, which is not new.

tau2 retail policy already requires the agent to get an explicit 'yes' from the user before consequential writes (shown in the tau2 policy text; worth confirming in the local copy). A gate that asks before irreversible calls overlaps behaviour the policy already rewards. A prompted 'confirm the exact arguments before any write' baseline may match it, and that baseline is not among the arms.

The only new part is the per-user probe refit each night, and the planned test does not measure it (shown). The k2_test uses fixed weights with no sleep LoRA and no refit. Refit appears only as a follow-up, and even there the pass mark is 'AUROC drop <= 0.05', not 'refit beats a probe trained once'. If the test passes, it confirms prior work, not this idea.
fixable_flaws: Novelty is overstated. Provenance at the argument level before execution is in 2607.01236, PACT (2605.11039) and PACE (2610.01349), with block-and-ask in 2607.01236. Probes that flag wrong tool-call arguments are in 2608.27750 and 2608.00218. The why_new text should credit these. Four of the candidate's own cited ids (2604.04651, 2607.10059, 2511.08798, 2606.11349) are missing from known-ids.txt, and SAGE-Agent's arXiv id is unverified. Check all of them before citing.

The equal-compute self-consistency gate is missing. Sample k=3 calls; if their key arguments disagree, ask using the two most common values. This uses the same redraft budget, needs no probe and no labels, and gives a real runner-up for free. It is the most likely arm to tie GP (suggested). It should replace GE as the main comparison.

'Always confirm irreversible calls' is missing as a baseline. It is the obvious thing a real assistant would do. The value GP adds is fewer questions at equal safety, so results should be reported as a Pareto curve (harmful executions vs asks per task), not as accuracy at one fixed fire rate.

Statistics: 40 tasks x 4 trials are not 160 independent pairs. Run McNemar or a paired bootstrap at the task level (average each task's 4 trials). A +6/160 gain (about 4 points) on 40 tasks has low power (suggested), so a null result would be weak evidence either way. Either pre-register the minimum detectable effect or add tasks, for example the airline domain or held-out retail seeds.

Label leakage: 'user correction or undo in the next turns' on tau2 comes from a Haiku user simulator, not from Ben. The probe may learn simulator quirks. Keep simulator-derived labels apart from env-diff and gold-action labels, and report AUROC for each label source.
Matching the fire rate to 10% of train calls lets arms with different precision look the same. Match on dev at equal ask rate per task, then report test results unchanged.

The runner-up value from top-k first-token re-scoring will often be junk, such as a near-duplicate address or a different tokenization (suggested). Report how often the runner-up is a valid entity from context or contacts, and fall back to the self-consistency second value.

Real-use volume: Ben probably makes about 0 to 10 irreversible calls a day, so 5 to 30 labels a day is optimistic. Under realistic volume a nightly refit fits a handful of positives. Use a shared prior probe (synthetic plus tau2) with per-user bias terms only, and test that, instead of a per-user logistic fit from scratch.
attack.fair_baseline: Same k=3 sampling budget, used as a self-consistency gate. Draft 3 calls from the shared KV prefix. If the key arguments (recipient, id, date, path) disagree on an irreversible call, or the call has an orphan argument under the same provenance rules, ask a question built from the two most common values; otherwise run the majority call. No probe and no nightly fit. Match the ask rate on dev. Also include 'always confirm irreversible calls' as the safety ceiling, and the provenance-only lesion. Of these, provenance plus self-consistency is the arm most likely to match GP.
attack.likely_effect: Provenance part: on real assistant tasks where the request is underspecified (several Sams, 'the doc'), it probably prevents a large share of wrong-recipient or wrong-file irreversible calls, maybe 30-60% of them, at roughly 0.1-0.3 extra questions per task (suggested, from the guardrail papers and the mechanism; untested on K2). Most of that also comes from provenance plus self-consistency without the probe. Probe part: on grounded-but-wrong tau2 retail calls, expected gain over self-consistency at equal ask rate is 0-3 points pass^1, which is below what 40 tasks can detect (suggested). Nightly per-user refit beating a probe trained once: no evidence; the expected gain is about 0 with realistic label counts (untested).
attack.improved_test:
Split it into two changes, tested one at a time on the small K2 setup. Fixed K2-3.7B weights, no sleep LoRA. Keep this separate from village-model results.

STEP 1: provenance gate, without the probe.
Data: use Claude Batches to write 300 email/calendar/files/git tasks with mock MCP tools and 3-8k contexts. Do NOT plant gaps. Make the tasks naturally messy instead: real-looking contact lists with near-duplicates, relative dates, several files matching a vague name, and some tasks that are fully specified. Run K2 on all of them. Label each irreversible call harmful or fine from the env diff against a gold end state written with the task, which Claude grades blind. Then add 100 planted-gap tasks, reported only as a separate sanity column. Split 100 dev / 200 test by task. Tune every threshold on dev only.
Arms, all with the same k=3 sampling budget and ask rate matched on dev:
- A0: prompt only.
- A1: always confirm irreversible calls.
- A2: self-consistency disagreement gate.
- A3: provenance only.
- A4: provenance plus self-consistency.
Main metric: harmful irreversible executions per 100 tasks, and asks per task, shown as a Pareto plot.
PASS (fixed in advance): A3 or A4 cuts harmful executions by at least 40% relative to A0, AND asks per task are at most half of A1's while keeping at least 80% of A1's harm reduction. Test with a task-level paired bootstrap, 95% CI excluding zero.
REFUTED: A2 alone gets within 10% of A4's harm reduction at the same ask rate (provenance adds nothing), or A4's over-asking on fully specified tasks exceeds 0.2 per task.

STEP 2: probe, only if Step 1 passes.
Score only calls that passed provenance and self-consistency, using the residual errors from Step 1 plus tau2 retail. On tau2 retail, use the 74/40 split, run 3 seeds of 40 test tasks, and analyse at the task level.
Arms at equal ask rate: A4 vs A4 + probe vs A4 + trap-type prior.
PASS: probe AUROC at least 0.72 on held-out calls, at least the type prior + 0.05, AND A4 + probe beats A4 by at least 5 points pass^1 (task-level CI excluding zero). Also report a prompted 'confirm exact arguments before any write' arm, because tau2 policy already requires confirmation.
REFUTED: AUROC below 0.65, or no pass^1 gain over A4 beyond 2 points.

STEP 3: the actual novelty claim.
Simulate 14 nights. Each night gets 10 labelled calls (realistic volume) drawn from a held-out 'user' with their own error mix, for example a habit of picking the wrong Sam. Each night also applies a small sleep-LoRA update.
Arms: probe trained once on synthetic data plus tau2 vs nightly refit on recomputed features with a shared prior plus per-user bias.
PASS: nightly refit beats the train-once probe by at least 0.05 AUROC on that user's day-15 calls.
REFUTED: the gap is below 0.02. In that case drop the nightly refit and keep the gate as a fixed component.

Cost: about 4 T4-h for Step 1 collection plus redraws; about 6 T4-h for Step 2, sharing collection with Tripwire; about 2 T4-h for Step 3. Claude about $12-18.

Plain-language summary for Ben: before the assistant does something it can't undo, it checks where each important detail came from, and asks you when it can't tell. First we test whether that check, on its own, stops real mistakes without asking you too often. Only if it does do we test the 'mistake detector' and whether retraining it each night actually helps.

candidates.name: Pointer-ledger folding, distilled nightly from the full-context self
candidates.one_line: Teach the small model at night to fold long tasks into a short append-only ledger whose entries keep exact handles and point back to raw turns, trained so its next action from ledger + recent turns matches what it did with the whole history in view.
candidates.mechanism: DAY: each long task keeps a LEDGER block after the stable system/tool prefix. When live context passes a fold budget F (e.g. 3k tokens past the ledger), the model writes one entry for the turns being folded: {id: T17-T24, did: <one line>, got: <exact handles: order ids, paths, message-ids, codes, numbers, names>, open: <pending>, constraints: <user rules>}. The raw turns leave the prompt but stay in the diary (FTS5) under their id. One new tool, expand(id), pastes the raw turns back for a single step. The ledger is append-only, so the prefix stays byte-stable and mlx_lm.server's exact-prefix cache keeps hitting. NIGHT (inside the normal sleep LoRA, KL anchor unchanged): from each day task longer than about 2F tokens, pick 4-8 fold points. Teacher = the same frozen base with the full raw history in context, used only on steps the run outcome or a Claude batch check marks correct. Targets: (a) WRITE: Claude (Batches) writes the ledger entry from the raw turns, and a string check confirms that every handle used in later turns appears verbatim in 'got'. (b) ACT: input = prefix + ledger + last k turns, target = the teacher's next action; if that action copies a string found in neither the ledger nor the last k turns, the target becomes expand(id_of_source) then the action. Loss only at target positions. LoRA on attention and MLP of K2-3.7B.
candidates.weak_spot: The teacher is the 3.7B's own full-context run, which is often wrong on 30k-token tasks, leaving fewer usable fold points biased toward easy tasks; Claude-fixed actions help but make it partly Claude distillation. The ledger may drop a handle that only matters 40 turns later, which the string check cannot predict. Synthetic mock-tool tasks may not match Ben's real email/calendar/coding logs.
candidates.why_new: MEM1 (2506.15841) and MemAgent (2507.02259) use RL and discard or overwrite history; CompactionRL (2607.05378) is RL summaries at 106B; 2608.06503 documents compaction instability; Sleep-time compute (2504.13171) rewrites context at idle time without training; project Notebook-1 showed notes lose specifics (ss-assistant 50 vs 90). New: no RL, supervised self-distillation from the model's own full-context run on the user's own logs inside the existing sleep loop; memory that is lossy for gist but lossless for specifics (verbatim handles plus a learned expand pointer into the diary), which answers the Notebook-1 failure; and an append-only layout that keeps the Mac's exact-prefix cache working, which rewrite-style summaries break.
candidates.k2_test: DATA (Claude Batches): 300 long tasks in a mock email/calendar/files/small-repo environment (deterministic Python tools, JSON state checker), 40-80 tool turns each, with 2-4 needles that appear early and are needed late (a confirmation code from turn 6 used at turn 50; 'never cc Dana' from turn 3). 180 train, 120 held-out. K2 full-context rollouts on train tasks (vLLM on T4, 16k) give teacher steps. ARMS at a 4k live-context budget except A: A = full context, no fold (upper bound and cost reference); B = sliding window + zero-shot ledger prompt; EQUAL-COMPUTE C = same LoRA, steps and tokens on plain full-context SFT of the same correct trajectories, served with the zero-shot ledger at 4k; D = pointer-ledger LoRA. One change C->D: the training targets. METRICS: task success, needle-use accuracy, mean prompt tokens per step, expand calls per task. PASS (PREREG, paired McNemar on 120 held-out, 2 seeds): D >= C + 10 task success (p<0.05); needle accuracy >= C + 15; D >= A - 5 at <= 40% of A's prompt tokens; tau2 retail 40x2 within 2 of C; ARC within 1. WRONG IF D - C <= 3, or D needs more than 1 expand per 5 steps (then it is retrieval, not memory).
candidates.mac_fit: SERVE: same nightly adapter. Live context capped near 4k plus ledger, so K2 cold prefill is about 10-15 s worst case vs about 50 s at 16k; warm turns hit the append-only cache (0.08 s TTFT measured). KV per agent shrinks about 4x, which is what lets 2-4 agents run side by side on the M1 Pro and keeps long tasks inside the 8 GB M2. expand(id) is an FTS5 lookup plus at most about 1-2k tokens of prefill for one step. NIGHT: about 10-20% more sleep steps; the teacher pass is forward-only and can run at q4 inside the capped Mac job (capped at 8k context on the 8 GB M2).
candidates.test_cost: About 9-10 T4-h per seed (3 h teacher rollouts, 2 training arms at about 1.5 h, about 3 h eval for 4 arms x 120 tasks); 2 seeds about 18-20 h, or seed 2 on the 5070 Ti. Claude Batches: about $5-8.

Each piece has prior art. Checked by reading abstracts (shown): ARC, TSUBASA, TTCD. Snippets only (suggested): AgentFold, Context-Folding, Source-Judged Compaction, AutoCompact, Agent Memory Distillation, DuoMem.

Known-ids check (/mnt/project-files/research/sweep-2026/known-ids.txt, 1082 lines): only 2504.13171 (Sleep-time compute) is present. Not present: 2506.15841 (MEM1), 2507.02259 (MemAgent), 2607.05378 (CompactionRL), 2608.06503, and every new id above (ARC, AgentFold, Context-Folding, TSUBASA, TTCD, Source-Judged, AutoCompact, etc.). The NIGHT self-distillation idea is partly already planned in-house. Item 21 (multi-night forgetting) also overlaps.

Recommended changes to the proposal, before any run:
1. Rewrite why_new. Drop the claim that the pointer/append-only layout is new (ARC has it). Keep the claim that the learned pointer plus distilled targets is new, if it holds after a search of 2026 OpenReview.
2. Add an arm that matches ARC: zero-training, append-only ledger plus expand(id), no LoRA. Without it, D-vs-C gains cannot be attributed to the training targets rather than to the pointer design. This is the main confound. The planned A-B-C-D set does not separate them.
3. Add TSUBASA/TTCD as the baseline for teacher-student distillation with a shorter student, so the novelty claim is measured against it.
4. The string check in the WRITE target is closely related to Source-Judged Compaction. Cite it and state what the check adds (training-time, not inference-time).
Limits: 6 web searches and 3 abstract fetches (via curl, not the docs tools). The Compaction Cliff (2608.22752) and Slipstream (2605.08580) surfaced in search but were not read. Not checked against OpenReview or GitHub beyond search snippets.

fatal_flaws: Mostly not new (shown by the prior-art check). ARC (2607.25066) already does the append-only, ID-addressable store with recall by ID. AgentFold and Context-Folding already fold context when it passes a budget. TSUBASA and TTCD already distill a full-context teacher into a shorter-context student. What is left is narrow: supervised targets for WRITE and ACT, taken from the model's own full-context run inside the sleep loop. Any claim has to be measured against that narrow piece, not the whole system.

The baseline is unfair, so the planned D-vs-C result cannot answer the question. C is trained on full-context inputs and then served at 4k with a ledger prompt it has never seen. D is trained on exactly the ledger-plus-recent-turns layout it is served with. A D>C gap would mostly measure format exposure (train/serve mismatch in C), not the self-distillation targets. And with no zero-training ARC-style arm (ledger + expand(id), no LoRA), nothing separates 'the pointer design helps' from 'the training helps'. Suggested, from the arm design itself.

The teacher signal does not exist the way the mechanism says it does in real use. Ben's day logs would be produced under folding, so the full-context action is a counterfactual that was never executed. 'Steps the run outcome marks correct' therefore does not apply to it. Only the Claude batch check can label it, which turns ACT into Claude-judged distillation on real logs. On the 8 GB M2 the night job is capped at 8k context, so the 'full-context teacher' is not full context for any task longer than 8k, which is exactly the tasks the method is for. Shown from the stated mechanism and limits.
fixable_flaws: The benchmark is built to favor the method. Every task has 2-4 needles that appear early and are needed late. Add long tasks with no needles, and coding tasks where the 'handles' are code spans rather than short IDs. Otherwise needle accuracy is graded on the method's home ground.

Observation masking is missing as a baseline: keep every action and reasoning line, replace old tool outputs with a stub plus expand(id). It needs no training and no summarizer, and published agent-context work (e.g. JetBrains' 'Complexity Trap', 2025) reports it matching LLM summarization. Suggested: on these tasks it may capture most of the gain.

A deterministic handle extractor is also missing as a baseline: regex/JSON pull of IDs, codes, paths and numbers from the folded tool outputs into 'got'. It is a cheaper WRITE than a learned or Claude-written entry, with zero hallucination.

Training and serving ledgers do not match. WRITE targets are written by Claude, but at serve time the 3.7B writes its own ledger. ACT inputs should include the student's own (imperfect) ledgers, or ACT will be trained on cleaner ledgers than it will ever see.

Teacher yield is untested. The 3.7B at 16-30k context on 40-80 tool turns may succeed rarely. Measure the fraction of fold points with a correct teacher action before training. Below about 30% of tasks, stop.

The A upper bound is weak. A 3.7B often gets worse with long context, so D >= A-5 may be trivial, and D may even beat A. Report A's raw success, and also an A' that uses a stronger reference (the 35B-A3B at full context) to show the headroom.

The Mac claims are unverified. The 0.08 s warm TTFT and the exact-prefix behavior of mlx_lm.server were not found in the repo notes, and the cache claim is half-true. Appending a ledger entry changes the bytes before the recent turns, so each fold re-prefills the last k turns (about 1-3k tokens), and each expand breaks the cache for that step and the next. Measure TTFT per step on the M1 Pro rather than asserting it.

The 'KV 4x smaller lets 2-4 agents run' claim mixes up two limits. Multi-agent decode tok/s on the M1 Pro is mostly bounded by memory bandwidth on the weights. KV size only matters at long contexts. The real win is prefill latency and the 8 GB M2 fitting. State it that way and measure tok/s per agent with 3 agents.

The expand-rate threshold is too loose. 1 expand per 5 steps on a 60-step task is about 12 expands, each with 1-2k tokens of prefill, which brings back a large share of the context cost. Also report the total tokens prefilled, including expands.
attack.fair_baseline: The fair baseline is zero-training infrastructure at the same 4k budget: an ARC-style append-only ledger whose 'got' field is filled by a deterministic handle extractor (regex/JSON over the folded tool outputs), the same expand(id) tool over the FTS5 diary, and observation masking of old tool outputs. On top of that, give it the same LoRA budget as plain SFT: inputs in the ledger + last-k layout, targets taken from the logged correct trajectory, no expand rewriting. Of the arms listed, this one would most likely match D. If it matches, the self-distilled targets add nothing.
attack.likely_effect: My guess is a small effect, with most of it coming from the zero-training parts. Suggested: going from a sliding window to ledger + expand with no training probably recovers most of the needle failures (+15-30 needle accuracy on this synthetic set), because ARC reports near-perfect recall by ID with plain prompting. Suggested: the self-distilled LoRA (D) over a format-matched SFT plus the deterministic ledger probably adds +2 to +6 task success on needle-heavy synthetic tasks, and about 0-3 on Ben's real email/calendar use, since most of those tasks are shorter than 2F (about 6k tokens) and never fold. Untested: coding tasks, where the 'handles' are code and expand would fire often, so it acts more like retrieval than memory. Shown: nothing yet. No arm has been run.
attack.improved_test:
STEP 0 (gate, about 2 T4-h): run K2 full-context rollouts on the 180 train tasks and count the fraction of fold points where the teacher action is correct, checked by the JSON state checker on a branch replay of that one step, not by outcome alone. Fixed in advance: if fewer than 30% of tasks give 4 or more usable fold points, stop and record the mechanism as not trainable at 3.7B.

DATA (Claude Batches): 120 held-out mock-env tasks with needles, plus 40 held-out long tasks with no needles, plus 30 long coding tasks in the small repo where later steps need exact code spans or paths from early reads. Same deterministic tools and checker for all. Train set as before (180).

ARMS, all at a 4k live budget except A, all served with the same expand(id) over the same diary:
A = full context, no fold (reference; also report A35 = Qwen3.6-35B-A3B full context as headroom).
M = observation masking: old tool outputs replaced by '[T17 output elided; expand(T17)]', actions kept, no training.
R = ARC-style: append-only ledger whose 'got' is filled by the deterministic regex/JSON handle extractor and whose 'did' is a one-line template, no training.
C' = same LoRA rank, steps and tokens as D. Inputs are prefix + R-style ledger + last k turns. Targets are the logged correct trajectory's actions, with no expand insertion and no self-teacher.
D = the full proposal, with ACT inputs built from the student's own ledgers (half Claude-written, half self-written).
One change from C' to D: where the targets come from (full-context self-teacher plus expand insertion), plus learned WRITE.

EQUAL COMPUTE: C' and D get identical optimizer steps, token counts and LoRA config. D's teacher pass and Claude ledger cost are reported separately as overhead.

METRICS: task success; needle-use accuracy; total prefilled tokens per task including expands; expand calls per step; on the M1 Pro, median and p95 TTFT per step and decode tok/s per agent with 3 agents running at once.

PASS (fixed in advance; paired McNemar, 2 seeds, both seeds must agree):
(1) D >= max(M, R) + 8 task success on the 120 needle set, p < 0.05.
(2) D >= C' + 5 task success, p < 0.05. This shows the targets matter, not the format.
(3) Needle accuracy D >= R + 10.
(4) No-needle set: D within 2 of the best other arm. Coding set: D >= R.
(5) D total prefilled tokens <= 40% of A's.
(6) Expands <= 1 per 8 steps.
(7) tau2 retail 40x2 within 2 of C'; ARC within 1.
(8) Mac: p95 TTFT <= 3 s and >= 30 tok/s per agent with 3 agents.

REFUTING RESULTS (any one counts):
- D - max(M, R) <= 3, which would mean the zero-training ledger is enough and training is not needed.
- D - C' <= 2, which would mean the gain is format exposure, not self-distillation.
- R >= A - 5 at <= 40% of A's tokens, which would mean the pointer design alone already solves the problem.
- Expand rate > 1 per 5 steps, which would mean it is retrieval, not memory.

Keep the village model and the small card experiments out of this test. Cost: about 12 T4-h per seed (5 arms of eval plus 2 training arms plus the gate), with seed 2 on the 5070 Ti; Claude Batches about $6-10.

The test above is built so that 'no' shows up clearly if that's the answer.

candidates.name: Ask once, then remember (regret/annoyance sleep with a Ben-twin follow-up)
candidates.one_line: Each night, find turns where the assistant guessed and Ben corrected it (train ask-over-guess on that slot) and turns where it asked about something it already knew (train act-over-ask). Ben's answer becomes a fact for the fact sleep, so the same question is never asked twice. Stage 2 adds a small 'Ben-twin' LoRA that predicts Ben's answer, so agents can fill a slot without asking when the twin's samples agree and the diary agrees with them.
candidates.mechanism: DAY: the diary already logs raw calls. NIGHT tagging (rules plus one Claude Batches pass): REGRET turn = the assistant committed a slot value (recipient, date, file, amount, which meeting) without asking, and within 3 turns Ben corrected it ('no, I meant...', undo or edit of the action, re-send to another address). ANNOYANCE turn = the assistant asked and the answer was already in context or in the diary (BM25 hit on the answer string), or Ben said 'obviously' / 'just do it'. TRAINING inside ab_ob_b4_nb with the same KL anchor, capped at about 15% of night steps so total compute is unchanged: (a) regret -> DPO pair, chosen = a one-line question naming the slot with the 2 most likely values as options (Claude writes it from the correction), rejected = the guessed action; (b) annoyance -> chosen = the direct correct action, rejected = the question; (c) Ben's answer or correction goes as a fact sentence ('Ben's "Mom" = ann.hannan@...; "the meeting" = Tuesday 4pm robotics') into the names re-read and fact-dream pipeline, and later turns on that slot become act-not-ask examples with an ask as the rejected side. Nothing is added at serve time. STAGE 2 (separate test, only if stage 1 passes): a second r16 LoRA, 'twin', on the same base, trained on 15% of night steps by role-swap (context -> Ben's actual next message), with Ben's answers to questions, corrections and draft edits upweighted 5x and recency weighting. At serve time, when the agent emits ASK(question), the gateway hot-swaps to the twin and samples k=5 answers (T=0.8, max 30 tokens). If at least 4 of 5 agree and no diary contradiction is found, the slot is filled silently and logged 'twin-filled'; otherwise Ben is asked. Irreversible actions always ask Ben. Overrides of twin-filled slots become 5x twin data and skill-sleep DPO pairs.
candidates.weak_spot: Labels are sparse and biased: a silent wrong action Ben never mentions gives no label, early nights have few pairs, and rule-based correction detection may mislabel ordinary follow-ups. DPO toward asking can spread into general over-asking unless annoyance pairs balance it. The twin can confidently agree on a stale preference after Ben changes his mind; agreement measures consistency, not correctness, so recency weighting and the diary check carry real load. The simulated Ben is tidier than the real one.
candidates.why_new: Abstain-R1 (2604.17073) and CIGAsk (2609.24290) train ask/abstain with verifiable or simulated-user rewards, online, at a fixed time. AgentAbstain (2607.10059) and Ask-or-Assume (2603.26233) are evaluations; the knowledge-boundary family (2604.14324, KARL 2604.22779) labels by QA correctness; SAGE-Agent (2511.08798) uses a hand-built EVPI model. User simulators and digital twins are used for evaluation, not as serve-time gates. The literature gap list names 'learning from the user's answers to clarifying questions as a nightly signal' and 'per-user ask-frequency calibration' as unstudied. New: slot-level labels from one real user's corrections and complaints, coupled to the fact sleep so a question becomes a remembered fact and the ask rate on recurring slots should fall each night; and (stage 2) a nightly per-user twin whose sample agreement gates asking, replacing 'am I sure?' with 'can I predict Ben?'. Nothing in the project's tried or queued lists trains asking.
candidates.k2_test: SIMULATED BEN (Claude Batches; K2-3.7B bf16 on Kaggle T4): a hidden persona with 60 slot facts (ambiguous nicknames, which 'meeting', default meeting length, which file is 'the essay', send-vs-draft rules) plus 8 preferences that change on day 8. 5 days x 40 requests over mock email/calendar/files tools, about 50% underspecified given what the model knows then. A Claude user-sim answers questions and writes corrections from the persona (2 Batches rounds per day). STAGE 1 ARMS, nights 1-5, same total steps and tokens: A = ab_ob_b4_nb on the same logs with corrected final actions as plain SFT; B = A + regret/annoyance DPO + answer-to-fact. Prompt-only reference row ('ask if any required detail is missing'). EVAL days 6-7, 120 fresh requests: 50 knowable (slot answered or corrected before; right move = act correctly), 50 new ambiguity (right move = ask about that slot), 20 fully specified (act). Score = right-move rate, graded by Claude Batches plus exact tool-argument match. PASS (PREREG): B >= A + 12 right-move (McNemar p<0.05, both seeds); B asks on <= 10% of knowable and fully specified items; ARC and fact recall within 2 of A; side check: ask rate on recurring slots falls from day 1 to day 5. REFUTED if B <= A + 4, or the gain comes only from asking more (over-asking on knowable > 20%, or no gain on the knowable subset). STAGE 2: 14 nights, S = stage-1 recipe with an own-probability ask gate tuned to T's ask rate, T = 15% of steps moved to the twin plus the twin gate. Pass: at matched ask rate T >= S + 10 slot accuracy, or T within 2 of S with <= 50% of S's questions; changed-preference accuracy T >= S. Refuted if twin-filled slots are wrong > 15% of the time.
candidates.mac_fit: STAGE 1 SERVE: zero cost (same LoRA, no extra tokens); fewer wrong actions and repeat questions should cut turns per task. NIGHT: about 50-300 short DPO pairs (<= 1k tokens), reference log-probs from the q4 base already loaded for the KL anchor; a few minutes of MLX time, fits the 5 GB-capped 8 GB M2. Detection is one Claude Batches call a night (about $0.05) or rules only offline. STAGE 2: twin adapter about 40 MB on the loaded K2 q4 base; adapter swap in ms with a shared prompt cache; 5 x 30 tokens batched is about 1.5 s on the M1 Pro and about 3 s on the 8 GB M2, only on ask events. The K2 twin can also gate Qwen3.6 agents.
candidates.test_cost: Stage 1: Kaggle T4x2 about 3-4 GPU-h generation plus 4-6 GPU-h nightly LoRA/DPO (5 nights x 2 arms x 2 seeds), about 8-10 h total; Claude Haiku 5.5 via Batches (Sonnet for persona) about $4-7. Stage 2: about 15 T4-h, Claude about $5-7 (live Ben-sim cannot be batched).

fatal_flaws: The stage-1 design gives the win to the wrong part of the idea. Arm B gets two things A does not: the ask/act DPO pairs and the answer-to-fact pipeline. The 50 'knowable' eval items are the very slots whose answers B was trained on as facts. So most of B's gain on knowable items will come from fact sleep, which is already adopted at 91% recall, and not from learning when to ask. A pass would not show that ask-training does anything (suggested; this follows from how the arms are built).

The fair baseline is missing: a small serve-time slot memory. Store each question and Ben's answer as a diary key-value entry and add the top 3 BM25 hits (about 150 tokens) to the prompt. That alone makes 'never ask the same question twice' nearly free, and it updates the moment Ben changes his mind, which a nightly LoRA cannot do. A design with no such arm cannot show that weights beat a lookup on this slice (untested, but very likely strong given how simple the slots are).

Stage 2 (the twin gate) does not justify its cost. Sample agreement measures self-consistency, not correctness. The twin shares a base with the agent, so their errors are correlated. Twin-2K-500 reports only about 72% per-person prediction accuracy even with rich personas. Stale preferences are exactly the case where a recency-weighted LoRA agrees confidently and is wrong. On the Mac, gating Qwen3.6-35B-A3B agents means keeping K2 q4 plus its KV cache resident next to about 20 GB of Qwen, so the 28 GB limit is tight with several agents (suggested). This is not fatal to stage 1, but stage 2 should be dropped from this candidate, not queued after it.
fixable_flaws: Compute matching is loose. 'Same total steps' should mean A spends the same 15% of night steps on extra fact-dream or SFT steps from the same corrections, not that it skips them. Otherwise B simply gets more targeted data.

No arm separates DPO from plain SFT on the chosen side. Add B-sft: the same chosen questions and actions as SFT, with no rejected side. Small-pair DPO under a KL anchor is fragile (see 2608.00301, abstention collapse). If B-sft matches B, the DPO machinery is not needed.
The 50% underspecified rate is far above real use (real is probably 5-15%). This inflates how much asking pays off and hides over-asking costs. Use about 15% in a second eval split.

Label precision is never measured. The rule-based regret/annoyance tagger may count ordinary follow-ups ('also cc Dad') as corrections. Hand-label 100 tagged turns from the sim, and later from real logs. Require precision of at least 0.8 before training on them.
Silent wrong actions produce no label. The eval should include items where the sim-Ben never corrects a wrong guess, to measure whether the sparse labels hide real errors.

Sparse-data risk on real use is not checked. Before any GPU spend, count regret and annoyance events in a week of Ben's real diary. If there are fewer than about 5 a night, the nightly DPO will be noise for weeks.
Two seeds on 120 items is thin for a 12-point margin across 3 subsets. Report subset CIs, and let the per-subset rules (not only the pooled score) decide the outcome.

Citations need fixing: 2511.08798 is ClarifyBench (uncertainty-weighted GRPO), not SAGE-Agent with EVPI. 2603.26233 proposes a scaffold, not only an evaluation. PAHF (2602.16173) already does ask-before-act plus memory updates from corrections, which narrows the novelty to 'nightly, in weights, with DPO'.

The 'right move' grade should not rest only on the Claude grader. For ask items, require the question to name the correct slot (exact slot-ID match from the persona). For act items, require an exact tool-argument match.
attack.fair_baseline: Arm A+: ab_ob_b4_nb with the same nightly steps. Corrected final actions go in as SFT. Ben's answers and corrections go in as fact sentences through the same names re-read and fact-dream pipeline, using the 15% step budget that B spends on DPO. Serve time adds a BM25 slot memory over past question/answer and correction diary entries (top 3, about 150 tokens), plus the one-line prompt rule 'if a required detail is missing and not in memory, ask one short question naming it'. My expectation (suggested): this matches B on the knowable and fully specified subsets and closes most of the gap on new ambiguity. That leaves only learned ask calibration on genuinely new ambiguity as the thing B must win on.
attack.likely_effect: In the sim, against the weak arm A as written: shown nowhere yet, but B beating A by 15-30 right-move points is suggested, mostly on knowable items via facts. Against the fair baseline A+ with slot memory and a prompt rule: the gain on knowable items is about 0 to 3 points (suggested). On new ambiguity, DPO ask-training could add 5-12 points if the 3.7B model under-asks with the prompt rule alone (untested). The over-asking risk on fully specified items is real, and the annoyance pairs only partly offset it (suggested). Real use for Ben is untested: likely a few fewer wrong-recipient or wrong-meeting actions per week, and data stays sparse for the first weeks. Stage 2 twin: untested, and I expect it to cost more than it gains (twin-filled error above 15% on changed preferences is likely).
attack.improved_test:
Step 0, free, run first. Pull 7 days of Ben's real diary. Run the tagger and hand-check 100 tagged turns. Gate: at least 5 regret+annoyance events a night and tagger precision of at least 0.8. If either fails, stop and drop the candidate.

DATA: the same Claude-Batches persona sim (60 slot facts, 8 preferences that change on day 8 kept for a later run), 5 days x 40 requests. Two eval splits on days 6-7. Split H: 120 items (50 knowable, 50 new ambiguity, 20 fully specified). Split R: 120 items at a realistic mix (about 15% new ambiguity, 35% knowable, 50% fully specified). Add 20 'silent-wrong' items where sim-Ben never corrects a guess. All eval slots and phrasings are unseen; new-ambiguity slots never appear in training.

ARMS (K2-3.7B on Kaggle T4, same night steps and tokens, 3 seeds):
- A+ = fair baseline: facts from answers + corrected-action SFT + BM25 slot memory + ask prompt rule.
- B = A+ with the 15% fact/SFT top-up replaced by regret/annoyance DPO.
- B-sft = like B, but chosen sides only, as SFT.
- P = prompt rule only, no night training (reference).

GRADING: an ask is right only if it names the correct persona slot ID. An act is right only on an exact tool-argument match. The Claude grader is used only to settle ties on free text.

PASS MARKS (fixed in advance):
1. On the Split H new-ambiguity subset, B >= A+ + 8 right-move (paired McNemar p<0.05, pooled over 3 seeds, and the sign holds in every seed).
2. On Split R overall, B >= A+ + 3, and B's ask rate on fully specified items is at most A+ + 3 points.
3. On knowable items, B >= A+ - 2.
4. ARC and fact recall within 2 of A+.
5. B beats B-sft by at least 3 on new ambiguity; otherwise adopt the cheaper B-sft.

REFUTED if any of these hold:
- B <= A+ + 3 on new ambiguity.
- B's gain on Split R is below 0 (over-asking eats the win).
- A+ answers knowable slots as well as B and B adds nothing elsewhere. Then the answer is memory, not ask-training, so ship the slot memory alone.

Stage 2 is removed from this test. If ever revisited, compare it first against an own-logprob gate at a matched ask rate on changed-preference slots only. Refute it if twin-filled slots are wrong more than 10% of the time.

COST: about 10-12 T4-h and about $5 in Batches. Run the Step 0 gate before any GPU time.

Plain-language summary for Ben: the part you would feel most ('don't ask me the same thing twice') is probably handled just as well by a small memory note the assistant reads before acting. The new and worth-testing part is teaching the model, overnight, when to ask about things it has never seen. The 'Ben-twin' that guesses your answers is the riskiest piece; drop it for now.

candidates.name: Sleep-grown macro tokens (per-user vocabulary that grows each night)
candidates.one_line: Each night, the most repeated multi-token spans in Ben's agent turns (tool-call JSON skeletons, file paths, his sign-off, calendar field names) become new single tokens trained inside the sleep LoRA, so one decode step can emit 5-20 real tokens, and unlike speculative decoding the gain does not shrink when 4-8 agents share a batch.
candidates.mechanism: NIGHT (after the normal ab_ob_b4_nb data is built): (1) Mine the day's diary JSONL, assistant turns only, for spans of 4-40 base tokens, ranked by count x (len-1) = decode steps saved. Drop spans containing a digit run, ID or email address seen fewer than 3 times. Append-only macro table capped at 1024 entries with fixed IDs, at most 128 new per night; a macro unused for 14 days is retired (row frozen and masked). (2) Add each macro as a row in K2's untied embedding and lm_head: embedding = mean of its parts; lm_head = the first part's row minus log(len), so the macro starts unlikely. (3) Re-tokenise all of tonight's training text (dreams, re-reads, skill-sleep data, KL-anchor prompts) with greedy longest-match on input and target. New rows train at 10x the LoRA LR alongside the usual LoRA. The KL anchor is computed over the base vocabulary by summing each macro's probability into its first base token. DAY: mlx_lm.server loads base q4 + LoRA + about 1024 extra fp16 embedding/head rows; the detokeniser expands macros. Prompts are macro-tokenised too, so tool blocks and repeated tool results get shorter (less prefill and KV per agent). The prompt cache is invalidated after each night.
candidates.weak_spot: (a) The gain sits in boilerplate; if Ben's turns are mostly prose, step savings may be only 15-25%. (b) Rows trained for one night may be undertrained, so the model emits a macro where the right tokens differed by one character (a wrong argument key), a correctness risk for tool calls. (c) The model cannot see inside a macro (spelling, partial edits of a path). (d) The table changes nightly, so the prompt cache must be rebuilt each morning.
candidates.why_new: zip2zip-style adaptive LZW hypertokens at inference and AdaptiVocab-style domain vocabulary expansion (2025, ids unverified). Speculative decoding and MTP were dropped in the project (verify cost r4=2.31 for 8B); D-cut (2607.14647) shows batched spec decoding falls below autoregressive at high concurrency and 2609.22156 bounds it on MoE. New: a per-user vocabulary grown nightly from the same diary the sleep reads, trained inside the KL-anchored sleep LoRA with an anchor kept well defined over the base vocabulary, aimed at agent tool-call boilerplate. The speedup is fewer steps per turn with no verify pass and no draft model, so it holds at high batch size, the one regime where this Mac (60-70 tok/s total plateau) currently loses.
candidates.k2_test: DATA: logged tau2 retail trajectories (Haiku 5.5 Scoreboard-1 runs and K2 skill-sleep runs) plus about 600 synthetic 'Ben's day' sessions (email triage, calendar edits, file ops, short coding) from Batches; 5 training 'days', 2 held-out days. ARMS (one change, equal optimizer steps and tokens seen): A = current sleep LoRA, base vocabulary, served with prompt-lookup n-gram drafting (best free speedup); B = same LoRA + macro tokens. METRICS on held-out days, teacher-forced from logged history: decode steps per assistant turn; exact match of the next tool call (name + args, JSON-normalised) and ROUGE-L of prose turns; tau2 retail pass^1, 40 tasks x 2 trials, K2 no-think. PASS (PREREG): B steps per turn <= 0.65x A; tool-call exact match within 2 of A (McNemar not significantly worse); tau2 within 2/80; simulated batch-4 throughput (steps x measured per-step cost at bs=4 on the T4) >= 1.4x A; recall and ARC within 1. REFUTED if the step ratio > 0.85, or exact match drops > 3 with most errors being wrong-macro choices.
candidates.mac_fit: SERVE: weights unchanged (K2 q4 about 2.6 GB + LoRA) plus about 1024 fp16 rows in embedding and head (well under 50 MB), fits the 8 GB M2. Per-step cost unchanged apart from a lm_head about 0.4% wider. Expected 1.4-2x real tok/s per agent on tool-heavy turns at 1, 2, 4 and 8 agents, with smaller KV and shorter prefill. The Qwen3.6 big tier could get the same table later. NIGHT: mining is CPU work (seconds to minutes); new rows train inside the existing sleep job with no extra steps; peak memory rises under 100 MB.

prior.notes:
Verdict: partly-new. Prior art covers the core mechanism. AdaptiVocab (2503.19693) does domain multi-token vocabulary expansion with blended embedding init and a light finetune, and zip2zip (2506.01084) does inference-time hypertokens. Neither is per-user or nightly, and neither uses a KL anchor defined over the base vocabulary. Searches found no paper that grows a per-user vocabulary from a daily log, retires macros, or measures steps-per-turn under batch-4 to 8 serving. Those are the parts that look new.

Key points for Ben and Astra:
1. Known-ids check. grep found 2609.22156 (line 1061) and 2404.19737 (line 296) in known-ids.txt. Not found: 2506.01084, 2503.19693, 2603.00030, 2509.18362, 2507.11851, 2410.17765, 2607.14647. The proposal cites zip2zip and AdaptiVocab as "ids unverified". Both ids are now verified and should be added to the sweep file. D-cut is cited in the proposal but is also missing from the file.

AdaptiVocab reports about 25% token reduction, which gives 1/0.75 = 1.33x, not the 1.4-2x claimed in mac_fit. Check whether the 1.4-2x figure assumes a bigger gain on tool-call boilerplate than prior art shows. The prior art was on niche prose or domain text, not agent tool calls.

4. The proposal's per-step cost claim (about 0.4% wider lm_head) is plausible, but nothing found tests it on the T4 at bs=4.

Sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2506.01084v2, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19693, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.00030, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.18362, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.11851, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14647.

fatal_flaws: Most of the claimed saving can be had without training, and the test leaves that option out (suggested). Tool-call JSON skeletons, field names and fixed keys are tokens a grammar already determines. Constrained decoding with jump-forward (SGLang's compressed-FSM style) adds them as one prefill-like chunk with no sampling step. Harness-side templating does the same job: the model emits name+args and the harness writes out the JSON. Neither needs new vocabulary rows, nightly retokenisation or a cache rebuild, and neither risks the model picking the wrong macro. Arm A is given only prompt-lookup drafting, which is itself spec decoding with a verify pass, so the project has already shown it loses at bs=4-8. A pass would therefore beat a baseline handicapped by design. Unless macros still save at least about 20% of steps after jump-forward removes the deterministic spans, the idea has no reason to exist (untested; it can be measured on CPU from the logs).

The main metric is teacher-forced 'decode steps per assistant turn'. That is just the tokenizer's compression ratio on logged text, which is known before any training. It says nothing about whether the model actually emits macros when generating freely. A model that never or rarely emits them, or emits the wrong one, would still 'pass' the 0.65x bar (shown by construction). Only free-running generation counts the real step saving. Without that the test cannot refute the claim.
fixable_flaws: Two changes are bundled. Macro-tokenising the prompts (tool results, history) alters what the model reads, and the rows have had only one night of LoRA training. That puts comprehension of emails, files and tool outputs at risk, and it bears directly on the recall numbers the sleep work depends on. Test output-side macros alone first. Prompt-side macros are a second, separate change (untested risk).

KL anchor alignment. Summing each macro's probability into its first base token gives the right marginal for the first token only. At positions inside a macro there is no student position to anchor, so the anchor silently covers fewer positions on exactly the text that is being changed. Fix: anchor only at macro boundaries, and report what fraction of anchor positions is lost (shown by the design's arithmetic).

The throughput check uses a T4 'simulated batch-4' number. The bottleneck being claimed is the Mac's 60-70 tok/s plateau with several agents. Measure wall-clock on the M1 Pro under mlx_lm at bs 1/4/8. The T4's per-step cost curve says nothing about Metal.

Wall-clock, not decode steps, is what Ben feels. Agent turns are often dominated by prefill of new tool results (emails, files) and by tool latency, and macros mined from yesterday barely compress that text. Report end-to-end seconds per completed task, not only steps per turn (suggested: the end-to-end gain is several times smaller than the decode-step gain).

The 1.4-2x expectation goes beyond any prior art. AdaptiVocab reports about 25% fewer tokens (about 1.33x at best). zip2zip v2 reports 15-40% (v1 said 20-60%; cite v2). SimpleTool's 4-6x applies only to the skeleton, not to whole turns. Pre-register the expectation at about 1.2-1.35x.

Serving engineering is unverified. mlx_lm.server needs a custom concat of q4 embedding/head plus fp16 rows. It also needs the detokeniser to expand macros before the tool-call parser and the chat-template stop tokens see them, plus streaming and partial-macro handling. All of this is feasible but untested on mlx and should be checked before any GPU spend (untested).

Interaction between nightly LoRA and the table. With fixed IDs, rows that persist across nights are retrained each night under a new LoRA. Retired rows stay in the head as masked logits. Nobody has stated whether yesterday's rows are reset or carried, and the two arms must be identical on this. 'Equal tokens seen' is also ambiguous because B has fewer tokens per document. Equalise on documents (the same text), not on token count.

Digits, IDs and emails are dropped only below 3 sightings. An order ID or address Ben uses often becomes a macro, and a near-miss (another order, another recipient) is then exactly the wrong-argument failure. Exclude all argument values from macros. Allow keys and structure only.
attack.fair_baseline: Same nightly sleep LoRA, base vocabulary, served with grammar-constrained tool-call decoding plus jump-forward: deterministic JSON skeleton and key spans are inserted as a single chunked forward, with no sampling steps. Optionally add a matched-budget LoRA that teaches a compact tool syntax (name(arg=val)) which the harness expands to JSON. This baseline costs zero extra training and adds no vocabulary risk. It is the most likely to match the macro arm on tool-heavy turns, because macros mined from boilerplate mostly duplicate what the grammar already forces.
attack.likely_effect: Suggested: compared with plain autoregressive decoding, output macros cut free-running decode steps on tool-heavy turns by about 20-35%, and on prose turns by about 5-15%. Compared with the jump-forward or compact-syntax baseline, the remaining saving is likely only 0-10% of steps. End-to-end wall-clock per completed assistant task at 4 agents improves about 0-8%, because prefill of new content and tool latency dominate. Untested: whether one-night-trained rows keep tool-call exact match within 2 points. The base-rate risk is a small but real increase in wrong-key or wrong-path errors. Prompt-side macros: untested, with plausible harm to comprehension and recall. Nothing here is shown on K2 or the Mac.
attack.improved_test:
This is the small K2 experiment, kept separate from any village or Qwen tier. One change at a time: output-side macros only, prompts stay in the base vocabulary.

STAGE 0 (CPU only, about 1 hour, no GPU, free). Data: 5 training days and 2 held-out days of real or synthetic Ben-day logs plus tau2 trajectories. Mine macros on the training days. On the held-out assistant turns, compute three numbers. (a) Raw token reduction from greedy longest-match. (b) The tokens that jump-forward under the tool-call JSON grammar would already force. (c) The residual saving: macro-saved tokens that are NOT grammar-forced, as a share of all assistant tokens. Pass mark fixed in advance: residual >= 20% on tool-heavy turns and >= 10% across all turns. REFUTED (drop the idea, no GPU spent) if the residual is < 12% across all turns.

STAGE 1 (Kaggle T4 for training, Mac for timing; about 4 T4-h plus about 2 Mac-h). Arms are equal in documents seen, optimizer steps and LoRA rank.
- A = sleep LoRA, base vocab, grammar-constrained jump-forward decoding.
- B = A + output macros: rows trained at 10x LR, argument values excluded from macros, KL anchored at macro boundaries.
- C (optional control) = compact-tool-syntax LoRA + jump-forward.
Metrics are all from FREE generation on the held-out days, never teacher-forced:
1. Decode steps per turn.
2. Next-tool-call exact match (name + JSON-normalised args) at 300+ held-out decision points, paired McNemar.
3. tau2 retail pass^1, 40 tasks x 3 trials, K2 no-think.
4. Macro misfire rate (macro emitted where the gold text differs).
5. Mac mlx_lm wall-clock per completed task at 1, 4 and 8 concurrent agents.
6. Fact recall and ARC.

PASS (pre-registered): B steps per turn <= 0.80x A; Mac wall-clock per task at 4 agents <= 0.88x A; exact match not significantly worse (McNemar p > 0.05) and drop <= 2 points; tau2 drop <= 3/120; misfire rate <= 1% of emitted macros; recall and ARC within 1.

REFUTED if any of these holds: B steps >= 0.90x A; wall-clock at 4 agents >= 0.95x A; exact match drops > 3 points with most errors at macro positions; C matches B on wall-clock within 3%. In that last case macros add nothing over the cheaper format change.

Prompt-side macros are tested only after Stage 1 passes, as their own one-change test with recall as the guard.

candidates.name: Tomorrow-first sleep (calendar-forecast dream selection)
candidates.one_line: Each night, rank which facts and two-hop pairs to dream by how likely Ben is to need them in the next 48 hours, from his own calendar, unanswered email and open tasks, so the fixed night budget goes to what tomorrow will ask instead of a random or coverage-ordered sample.
candidates.mechanism: STORED: nothing new at serve time; same diary and LoRA. NIGHT, before the ab_ob_b4_nb dream stage: (1) Build a 'tomorrow context' T from local data only: calendar events in the next 48 h (title, attendees, location, notes), email threads whose last message is to Ben with no reply, open todos and unfinished agent tasks from today's log, and a decayed copy of the last 3 days' recurring topics. (2) Take the candidate pool the recipe already builds (tagged one-hop facts and two-hop bridge pairs). (3) Score each candidate by BM25 against T plus a bonus when an entity is an attendee or sender in T; a two-hop pair is scored by its weaker hop. (4) Reallocate the fixed budget (4x work at s=4): 60% of dream and re-read steps go to top candidates ranked by score x (1 - current closed-book recall probability from a cheap probe), 40% to the normal replay mix so old facts are not starved. The names re-read pass is limited to names in T or the top candidates. Same LoRA targets and KL anchor; only item selection changes. Optional later extra, not tested here: a 300-token 'today card' of top forecast facts in the cached system prefix.
candidates.weak_spot: Requests that nothing on the calendar predicted get less night work, so recall on surprise questions could fall. In a synthetic world tomorrow can be too predictable, because one generator wrote both calendar and questions. The real gain depends on Ben keeping a calendar and inbox the assistant can read; if most requests are coding with no calendar trace, T is weak and the method falls back to recency.
candidates.why_new: Sleep-time Compute (2504.13171) precomputes context for predicted queries in the prompt, with no personal calendar and no weight training. SuRe surprise replay and FadeMem decay replay pick items by past signals (surprise, age). The project's queued 'dream uncovered two-hop pairs first' orders by coverage. No found paper or project note picks replay items by a forecast of one user's next-day needs from his own schedule. Since two-hop correct ~= pairs dreamed (measured), spending coverage on the pairs that will be asked should matter more than raising coverage overall, and it feeds long-task memory because an open task's facts are re-learned the night before it resumes.
candidates.k2_test: DATA (Claude Batches): a 14-day 'Ben-like week x2' world with about 60 people and projects, daily diary logs in the Sleep-B week format, and a calendar and inbox per day. A SEPARATE Claude call that sees the full world writes each day d+1's questions: 60% grounded in day d+1 events (meeting prep, two-hop like 'which room is the meeting with my sister's tutor in?'), 40% unscheduled old facts. Freeze and hash generator outputs before the run. ARMS on K2-3.7B fp16, closed-book, 14 nights, identical optimizer steps and tokens per night (logged and checked): C = ab_ob_b4_nb + queued coverage-first two-hop ordering; F = same recipe with forecast selection (the only change). Oracle arm (selection by the true next-day questions) on one seed as a ceiling. METRICS: next-day scheduled-question accuracy (closed book and with diary), two-hop accuracy on next-day pairs not verbatim dreamed in either arm, unscheduled accuracy, ARC, base diary reading. PASS (PREREG): F >= C + 10 on next-day scheduled questions (paired McNemar p<0.05 pooled over days 8-14, both of 2 seeds); unscheduled within -3; ARC within 1; diary reading >= C - 2. REFUTED if F - C <= 3 on scheduled questions, or unscheduled drops > 5 (gain bought by forgetting).
candidates.mac_fit: SERVE: zero extra cost. NIGHT: BM25 scoring of a few thousand candidates under 5 s on the M1 Pro plus about 200 short recall-probe forwards (under a minute at about 300 tok/s prefill). Training steps unchanged, so the night budget is the same on the M1 Pro and the 8 GB M2. Needs read-only local access to calendar and mail, which the gateway already logs.
candidates.test_cost: Claude Batches: world and about 1,700 questions about $3-4, grading about $1. GPU: 2 arms x 2 seeds x 14 nights about 14 T4-h, oracle arm about 3.5 h more; or about 1/3 the hours on the 5070 Ti when free.
