prior.notes:
Verdict: partly-new. Components are covered. Nothing found picks replay items by a forecast of one user's next-48h needs from calendar, email and tasks. Searches run: 5 web searches, 1 fetch (MSSR abstract only). Search gaps: no full-text read of SPRInG, ProMemAgent, MSSR or the 2606.03979 sleep paper; no arXiv/OpenReview query on "anticipated query rehearsal" or "temporal replay buffer" beyond the first pass.

Known-ids check (grep -c on /mnt/project-files/research/sweep-2026/known-ids.txt): 2504.13171=1, 2511.22367=1, 2603.09892=1, 2511.06446=1, 2606.03979=1, 2605.29495=1, 2607.16256=1, 2607.15587=1. Not present: 2601.09974 (SPRInG), 2610.27400 (ProMemAgent), 2607.21635 (user-conditioned eval of personal agents, temporal interventions; relevant to test design), 2509.23773 (knowledge homophily).

Overlap with the project's own notes (/home/user/learner/RANKING.md, BRIEF.md): RANKING item 1 ('graph-walk two-hop dreams') orders by graph path, not forecast. The 'dream uncovered pairs first' coverage ordering is not in the files I grepped, so it is taken from the task text only. The proposal's claim that two-hop correct ~= pairs dreamed is in RANKING.md line 7. Item 9 in RANKING.md (multi-night forgetting) is the nearest sibling for the 40% old-fact replay share.

Risks for the proposal, from the search: (a) the sleep-time compute result suggests predictability matters, so the forecast may help only where T is predictable (the proposal's own weak spot); (b) MSSR is the closest prior for the recall-probe term, so the reallocation half should cite it and not claim novelty; (c) the test's pass marks and the separate oracle arm are sound. Action items: add 2601.09974 and 2610.27400 to known-ids.txt, and read the MSSR full text before claiming the probe-based reallocation as new.

fatal_flaws: Leakage in the proposed test (untested, but the design guarantees it): one Claude call writes the calendar and inbox, and a second call that 'sees the full world' writes day d+1's questions, 60% of them 'grounded in day d+1 events'. The forecast T and the scheduled questions then share the same entities and words by design, so BM25 against T works almost like an oracle. A +10 win in that world shows that 'training on items close to the test helps', which is already known from the project's own 'two-hop correct ~= pairs dreamed' finding. It does not show that a calendar predicts Ben's real requests. As written, a pass cannot tell forecasting apart from peeking.

The baseline is wrong as specified (suggested). C is 'coverage-first' ordering, which purposely spreads the budget away from recent and active entities. Most of what the forecast picks is recent: today's unanswered email, unfinished tasks, and a decayed copy of the last 3 days' topics. A plain recency-weighted or 'entities touched in the last 72 h' selection, with the same 60/40 split and the same 1 - recall weighting, would probably match F at equal compute. Without that arm, any F > C gain cannot be credited to the calendar.
fixable_flaws: Novelty is overstated (shown, from prior art). Human sleep research shows that sleep preferentially strengthens memories people expect to need (Wilhelm et al. 2011, J Neurosci, 'Sleep selectively enhances memory expected to be of future relevance'). Spaced-repetition schedulers that work toward an exam date do the same thing for flashcards. Sleep-time Compute anticipates future queries. MSSR covers the 1 - recall reallocation. The new part is narrower: using one user's own calendar, email and tasks to choose LoRA replay items. Claim only that, and cite MSSR for the probe term.

Two factors are mixed into one arm (shown, from the design). F changes the forecast score AND adds 1 - recall weighting AND narrows the names re-read pass, all together. That breaks the project's one-change-at-a-time rule. Split them: a W arm (1 - recall only, no forecast) and an F arm that keeps the names re-read pass the same as C.

Much of the overlap is already handled (suggested). Today's facts get night work in both arms because the recipe trains on the day's log. So F can only win on OLD facts that come back tomorrow (old contacts in a meeting, a task resumed after days). The test must report that slice on its own (age of the needed fact >= 3 days), or the headline number is diluted or inflated by facts both arms already learn.

The comparison that matters in real use is missing (suggested). The assistant has calendar and email tools at serve time, and the forecast is equally available then. A 300-token 'today card' built from the same forecast (the deferred extra), or a quick diary search keyed on tomorrow's attendees, costs no training and could match F. A no-train card arm P, and F+P against P, should be in the test, or the weight-training half has no reason to exist.

The synthetic tomorrow is too predictable (suggested). Real calendars contain cancellations, unlisted meetings and requests that have nothing to do with the calendar. Ben is a high-school senior whose main daily traffic is coding and Schoology, so many days will have no calendar trace at all. The world generator should add noise: about 25% of calendar items cancelled or moved, about 30% of next-day requests that appear nowhere in T, and some days with an empty calendar.

The tolerance for unscheduled questions is too loose and is measured too early. The worry is slow loss of facts nobody asks about. Fourteen nights with 40% normal replay may not show it. Track how unscheduled accuracy changes for facts introduced in week 1 and checked on days 12-14, and refute if F's trend is worse than C's by more than 3 points.

Statistical power and day effects: pooling McNemar tests over days 8-14 treats questions as independent even though they cluster by day and by entity. Use a paired bootstrap over days and entities, or a mixed model, and report the result per day.
attack.fair_baseline: The fair baseline is a recency-plus-weakness selection. It uses the same fixed night budget, the same 60/40 split and the same 1 - closed-book-recall weighting, but ranks candidates by how recently they appeared in the logs (last 72 h, decayed) instead of BM25 against the calendar, email and task forecast. That is MSSR-style weakness scheduling plus recency, with no calendar input. A second fair comparator is the no-train version: the same forecast turned into a 300-token today card in the cached prefix, on top of the C recipe. Either one is the most likely to match F.
attack.likely_effect: Untested, so all of this is a guess. On the synthetic world as written, F - C is likely +8 to +15 on scheduled questions, mostly through leakage, so it would pass. Against a fair recency-plus-weakness arm in a noisy world, expect +0 to +4 on scheduled questions overall and perhaps +5 to +8 on the slice of old facts that return tomorrow. That slice is the only place a calendar holds information that recency lacks (suggested). In real use on Ben's Mac, the effect is probably small (suggested): most of his requests are coding or school work with little calendar trace, and the agent can already read the calendar and email with tools at serve time. A today card would probably capture most of whatever gain remains. Expect a measurable gain only on meeting-prep and resumed-task questions that need old diary facts, a few percent of his daily requests.
attack.improved_test:
STAGE 0 (no GPU, about one evening, run first as a go/no-go gate on real data): take 10-14 days of Ben's real gateway logs. For each day d, build T_d from the calendar, email and tasks as they stood at 23:00, plus a recency set R_d (entities from the last 72 h). On day d+1, tag the entities in Ben's actual requests, using Claude Batches to tag. Measure the forecast hit rate: the share of next-day requests whose entity is in T_d's top-k but NOT in R_d's top-k at equal k. PASS mark fixed in advance: at least 15% of requests reach for an old fact (age >= 3 days) that T ranks in the top-k and R does not. REFUTED or dropped if that share is under 5%. Either way, the calendar adds nothing over recency for Ben, and no GPU time is spent.

STAGE 1 (K2-3.7B fp16, run only if Stage 0 passes). DATA: a 14-day world about 60 people and projects, made in three separately frozen and hashed Claude calls. (a) A world and plan generator writes the calendar, inbox and tasks. (b) A 'reality' generator turns each plan into what actually happened on day d+1: about 25% of calendar items cancelled or moved, about 30% of requests unrelated to the plan, 2 days with an empty calendar. (c) A question writer sees ONLY the realized day d+1 transcript and the world fact table, never the calendar or inbox. It writes about 120 questions per day, each tagged with the age of the fact it needs and whether it is one-hop or two-hop. Leakage check fixed in advance: the mean BM25(question, T_d) must not exceed the same score measured on Stage 0 real data by more than 1.5x. Otherwise regenerate.

ARMS, all with the same optimizer steps, tokens per night, LoRA targets and KL anchor (logged and asserted), 14 nights, 3 seeds:
- C: the current recipe plus coverage-first ordering.
- W: C plus 60% of the budget on 1 - recall weighting (weakness only).
- R: like W but ranked by recency x (1 - recall).
- F: like W but ranked by forecast x (1 - recall). The names re-read pass is identical to C's.
- P: C plus a no-train 300-token today card from the same forecast.
- F+P.
- Oracle selection by the true next-day questions, on 1 seed.

METRICS: accuracy on next-day questions, split into old facts (age >= 3 days) and new facts; two-hop accuracy on next-day pairs not verbatim dreamed in any arm; unscheduled accuracy; the trend on week-1 facts checked on days 12-14; ARC; diary reading. Statistics: paired bootstrap over days x entities.

PASS (all fixed in advance): F >= R + 5 AND F >= W + 5 on old-fact next-day questions, with the 95% CI excluding 0, in all 3 seeds. Unscheduled accuracy >= C - 3, with the week-1 trend no worse than C by more than 3. ARC within 1. Diary reading >= C - 2. F+P >= P + 3; otherwise the training half adds nothing beyond the card. REFUTED if F - R <= 2 (recency explains the gain), if F+P - P <= 1 (the card makes the training unnecessary), or if unscheduled accuracy drops by more than 5. COST: Stage 0 under $2 of Batches and no GPU. Stage 1 about $6 of Batches and about 6 arms x 3 seeds x 14 nights, roughly 45 T4-h, which is 1.5 Kaggle weeks, or about 15 h on the 5070 Ti. To save GPU time, drop P and F+P to 1 seed. Summary for Ben in plain language: first check on your real days whether your calendar tells us anything that 'what you touched recently' doesn't. Only if it does, test it in a fake world where the person writing the quiz never sees the calendar.

ranking.name: Ask once, then remember (stage 1 only: ask/act preference sleep; twin removed)
ranking.reason: It goes after the weak spot Ben would notice most (guessing wrong, or asking twice) and has the best real-use score of the set (7). It is fairly new: nightly ask-vs-act training from one user's own corrections, tied into the fact sleep. It costs nothing at serve time on either Mac and fits under 6 T4-h if the world is kept small. The advisor's fixes turn it into a clean single-change test: an A+ arm with slot memory and a prompt rule, B against B-sft, a realistic ask mix, and grading by slot ID. Stage 2 (the Ben-twin) is dropped.

ranking.name: Recall-Then-Read, stage 1 only (slept LoRA as diary search-key writer)
ranking.reason: Cheapest real test of the two-hop weak spot. It is inference only and reuses the ab_ob_b4_nb LoRAs, at about 2-3 T4-h. The serve side is close to GenRead/HyDE/Query2doc, so only the 'weights hold hop 1' case is new. The fixed test isolates that case with condition W and fair two-round retrieval and alias-table arms. Stage 2 (cue-sleep) waits until stage 1 passes, and should cite Ma et al. 2305.14283 and DeepRetrieval 2503.00223.

ranking.name: Error-and-provenance gate
ranking.reason: High real-use value: it stops sends to the wrong Sam and deletes of the wrong file. Step 1 (provenance plus a self-consistency gate) is cheap and needs no training. Novelty is low, though: argument provenance is in 2607.01236, PACT and PACE, and tool-error probes are in 2608.27750. The only new part, the nightly per-user refit, likely gains about 0 at real label volumes. It also overlaps pick 1 on ask-vs-act. Worth building as plain engineering, but it is not a research pick.

ranking.name: Tripwire lines
ranking.reason: The novelty is real (the model fires its own trap cue, trained on fire-on-success and no-fire examples). But the advisor's fair arms (C0+, R, P, T-gen) and clustered statistics push the cost to about 20 T4-h and $25-35. The expected gain over C0+ or the prompt list is 0-4 pp, which 40 tasks cannot detect. It should wait until the skill-sleep thread reports.

ranking.name: Tomorrow-first sleep
ranking.reason: Good Mac fit, and Stage 0 is a free go/no-go on real logs. But a recency-plus-weakness ranking probably explains most of the gain. Ben's traffic is mostly coding and school work with little calendar trace. A today-card in the prompt probably captures what is left. The full Stage 1 is about 45 T4-h. Run Stage 0 only, whenever 10+ days of real logs exist.

ranking.name: Pointer-ledger folding
ranking.reason: ARC (2607.25066) already covers the append-only ledger and expand(id), and the zero-training arms (masking, a regex ledger) likely capture most of the gain. The 3.7B full-context teacher may rarely be right, and the 8 GB M2 night cap of 8k context breaks the 'full-context' teacher. A better first move is to adopt the zero-training ledger as engineering.

ranking.name: Alias-to-Entity State Tying (ASTie)
ranking.reason: The mechanism is interesting, but real use is weak (3). The serve-time alias line and deterministic alias substitution are near-free rivals that also handle changed links. The pre-gate as written cannot pass because it runs on the base model. With all fixes it costs about 15 T4-h. It only wins in a cross-day, text-deleted case that may not exist in Ben's setup.

ranking.name: Sleep-grown macro tokens
ranking.reason: The decode-step saving is mostly already available from grammar jump-forward or harness templating, with no vocabulary risk. The end-to-end gain at 4 agents is about 0-8%. It also risks wrong-argument tool calls. Its CPU-only Stage 0 can be run for free as a sanity number, but it is not a pick.

picks.name: Ask once, then remember: ask/act preference sleep (stage 1)
picks.mechanism: NIGHT, inside the existing KL-anchored sleep LoRA (ab_ob_b4_nb, r16, attention+MLP, same anchor on 100 general prompts). (1) TAG the day's diary with a rule pass plus one Claude Batches pass. A REGRET turn: the assistant committed a slot value (recipient, date, file, amount, which meeting) without asking, and within 3 turns Ben corrected it or the action was undone or re-sent. An ANNOYANCE turn: the assistant asked about a slot whose answer was already in context or in the diary (BM25 hit on the answer string), or Ben said 'obviously' or 'just do it'. (2) BUILD PAIRS. Regret gives a DPO pair: chosen = a one-line question naming the slot with the 2 most likely values (written by Claude from the correction), rejected = the guessed action. Annoyance gives a DPO pair: chosen = the direct correct action, rejected = the question. (3) Ben's answer or correction becomes a fact sentence ('Ben's "Mom" = ann.h@...') for the names re-read and fact-dream pipeline. This step is shared by all arms and is not the change under test. (4) These pairs take a fixed 15% slice of the night's compute. In the fair baseline, the same slice goes to extra fact and corrected-action SFT. SERVE, identical in every trained arm: a BM25 slot memory over past question/answer and correction diary entries (top 3, about 150 tokens) plus a one-line rule: 'if a required detail is missing and not in memory, ask one short question naming it'. No serve-time cost is added on top of the baseline. Irreversible actions are not treated specially here; that belongs to the separate provenance-gate work. The Ben-twin (stage 2) is removed.
picks.why_new: Prior ask/clarify training uses simulated or verifiable rewards online, at a fixed time: Abstain-R1 2604.17073, CIGAsk 2609.24290, the future-turn DPO of 2410.13788 (already in known-ids), and ClarifyBench 2511.08798 (which is uncertainty-weighted GRPO; the candidate wrongly called it SAGE-Agent/EVPI). PAHF 2602.16173 asks before acting and updates memory from corrections, but in-context, not nightly in weights. AdaMem 2606.21144 learns memory from corrections, with no ask-vs-act policy. Ask-or-Assume 2603.26233 is a scaffold. New here: slot-level ask/act preference labels mined from one real user's corrections and redundant questions, trained nightly inside the KL-anchored sleep LoRA, and tested against a strong memory-plus-prompt baseline. The question is whether learning WHEN to ask about unseen ambiguities adds anything beyond 'remember the answer'. The project's tried and queued lists contain no ask-training item (prior-art check, notes only). This is a lead from 8 searches, not proof. Fetch the full text of PAHF and AdaMem before claiming novelty in any write-up.
picks.prereg:
SCOPE: small K2-3.7B simulated-assistant experiment only. Keep it separate from the card experiments and the village model. Stage 2 (twin) is not part of this pre-registration.

STEP 0 (free, no GPU). If 7 or more days of Ben's real gateway diary exist, run the tagger on them and have Ben hand-check 100 tagged turns (about 20 min with a yes/no sheet). Gate: at least 5 regret+annoyance events per night on average, and tagger precision of at least 0.8. If real logs exist and either gate fails, stop: nothing is trained and the candidate is dropped for real use. If fewer than 7 days of real logs exist, the simulated test below may run, but any adoption decision waits for this gate. That is stated in the result.

TASK MATCHING REAL USE. A mock email/calendar/files assistant with deterministic Python tools (send_email, draft_email, create_event, move_event, open_file, share_file). The Claude-built persona 'sim-Ben' has 60 slot facts: ambiguous nicknames with several contacts, which 'meeting', default meeting length, which file is 'the essay', send-vs-draft rules. It also has 40 neutral background facts. The world runs 5 training days x 40 requests, about 50% underspecified given what the model knows at that point. The 8 changing preferences are dropped (they belong to a later multi-week run).

DATA SOURCE (Claude Batches). Sonnet writes the persona and request stream. Haiku 5.5 is the user sim, run in 2 Batches rounds per day: round 1 answers the agent's questions; round 2 writes corrections. A correction is triggered DETERMINISTICALLY when the committed slot value differs from the persona's value, and Claude only phrases it. Day logs are made once by base K2 (fp16, served with the prompt rule, T=0.7, fixed seed) and are SHARED by all arms. This offline design means each arm learns from identical days. It is a stated limitation, since on-policy days come later. Training labels come from the REAL tagger run on these logs, not from oracle labels. Tagger precision and recall against the deterministic oracle are reported.

EVAL (days 6-7, all slots and phrasings unseen). Split H, 200 items: 80 knowable (slot answered or corrected on days 1-5, so the right move is to act with the correct value), 80 new ambiguity (a slot never seen in training, so the right move is to ask about it), 40 fully specified (act). Split R, 200 items at a realistic mix: 15% new ambiguity, 35% knowable, 50% fully specified. Silent-wrong, 20 items: the model guessed earlier and sim-Ben never corrected it. Also 100 general non-assistant prompts to measure the general ask rate. GRADING: an ASK is right only if it names the correct persona slot ID, which a Haiku grader maps to one of the 60+N slot IDs (exact-match check; grader agreement measured on 60 items against a Sonnet regrade, kappa reported). An ACT is right only on an exact tool-argument match (JSON-normalised, NFKC). The Claude grader settles free-text ties only.

ARMS. All trained arms use the same base, LoRA config, KL anchor, 5 nights, optimizer steps, and compute measured in token-passes: a trained token counts 3 units (forward+backward), a reference-only forward token counts 1 unit. They also use the same number of Claude Batches calls per night (B's calls write the chosen questions; A+'s calls write the same number of fact and SFT paraphrases), and the same serve stack. All night compute is logged and asserted equal within 5%.
- A+ (fair equal-compute baseline): ab_ob_b4_nb + answers-as-facts + corrected-action SFT. The 15% slice is extra fact/SFT top-up from the same corrections. Serve: slot memory + prompt rule.
- B (the one change): A+ with the 15% slice replaced by regret/annoyance DPO (beta 0.1, reference = that night's starting adapter).
- B-sft: the same 15% slice as SFT on the chosen sides only.
- P (reference, untrained): base K2 + slot memory + prompt rule.
SEEDS: 2 (seeds 1 and 2 change LoRA init, data order and dream sampling; the day logs stay fixed).

METRICS. Right-move rate per subset and split; ask rate on fully specified, knowable and general prompts; silent-wrong accuracy; one-hop fact recall on the 100 slot+background facts; ARC-Easy (fixed 500-item subset); the trajectory of DPO reward margin and KL per night (to watch for the collapse described in 2608.00301).

PASS MARKS (fixed in advance; paired McNemar on the 160 pooled paired items of 2 seeds x 80, exact two-sided):
1. Split H new ambiguity: B >= A+ + 8 points, p < 0.05 pooled, and the sign is positive in BOTH seeds.
2. Split R overall: B >= A+ + 3 points, and B's ask rate on fully specified items is at most A+'s + 3 points.
3. Knowable: B >= A+ - 2 points.
4. ARC within 1 point and fact recall within 2 points of A+; general-prompt ask rate at most A+'s + 3 points.
5. B >= B-sft + 3 on new ambiguity. If B-sft also meets marks 1-4, adopt B-sft instead (cheaper and more stable).
All five must hold for B to be adopted. P is reported as a reference row only.

RESULT THAT PROVES IT WRONG (any one): B <= A+ + 3 on new ambiguity; B's Split R change below 0 (over-asking eats the gain); B more than 5 below A+ on knowable items. Diagnostic, not a pass mark: if A+ matches B everywhere, the useful part is the slot memory, so ship the memory and the rule without ask-training. If tagger precision on the sim is below 0.8, the result is flagged as label-noise-limited, and a follow-up on oracle labels is allowed only as a diagnosis.

COMPUTE PLAN (Kaggle T4x2, fp16; one arm-seed job per GPU so the two run in parallel). Day-log collection with base K2 on vLLM: about 0.4 GPU-h. Timing pilot: night 1 of A+ seed 1. If one night takes more than 9 min, cut dream and re-read counts EQUALLY in every arm until it fits. Training: 3 trained arms x 2 seeds x 5 nights x about 8 min = about 4.0 GPU-h. Eval: 4 arms x 2 seeds x (420 decisions + 100 general + recall + ARC) with short decodes = about 0.6 GPU-h. TOTAL about 5.0 GPU-h, hard cap 6.0. The PC 5070 Ti is an optional backup for one seed. API via Batches: persona and requests about $1.5; user sim 10 rounds about $1.5; tagging, pair writing and paraphrases about $1; grading about $1. TOTAL about $5.

picks.risks: (1) Offline shared day logs mean the arms never live with the results of their own asking. Real on-policy gains may differ (untested). (2) With small DPO slices under a KL anchor, the reward margin can collapse or over-asking can spread to general prompts. Watch the per-night margin and the general-prompt ask rate. (3) The sim may be tidier than real Ben. Its 50% underspecified training rate inflates the label count compared with the real 5-15%. Split R and the Step 0 gate are the checks. (4) The grader that maps a free-text question to a slot ID can be wrong. Kappa is reported, and the result is suspect if kappa is below 0.7. (5) The budget is tight: if the timing pilot shows nights over 9 min, the world shrinks, which weakens the fact-sleep part equally in every arm. (6) The 80-item new-ambiguity subset over 2 seeds gives limited power for +8. A null result near +5 is weak evidence either way. (7) A good result is still only shown for K2-3.7B in a simulated world, not for Qwen3.6 or real use.

picks.name: Recall-Then-Read, stage 1 (slept LoRA writes diary search keys; base reads)
picks.mechanism: SERVE only, no new training. The trigger is a memory question whose plain FTS5 hit on the raw question is weak; in the test, every two-hop item. (1) KEY PASS, LoRA ON: a fixed 1-shot prompt asks the slept K2 for up to 4 bridge names and short facts in at most 40 tokens, greedy ('my sister -> Maya; Maya -> dentist Dr. Lee'). (2) RETRIEVE: BM25/FTS5 over the day-by-day diary, with queries {question} plus each key, merged by reciprocal-rank fusion and trimmed to the same 1.5k k_tokens budget as the plain-diary arm. (3) READ PASS, LoRA OFF (base reader): answer from the retrieved turns. The main arm uses all keys (tau = -inf); a logprob gate is only an ablation. The idea under test: the weights act as a memory of WHICH names to search for (hop 1), while values are read from the diary. That matters most when hop 1 is no longer findable by search (condition W). Stage 2 (nightly cue-sleep on a hit@3 reward) is out of scope until stage 1 passes. If it is ever run, it must cite query-rewriter training on retrieval reward (Ma et al. 2305.14283, DeepRetrieval 2503.00223).
picks.why_new: Producing retrieval text from parametric knowledge is prior work: GenRead 2209.10063, Recitation 2210.01296, HyDE 2212.10496, Query2doc 2303.07678, Generate-then-Ground 2406.14891, and IRCoT 2212.10509 and Self-Ask 2210.03350 for iterative retrieval. These must be named as the main baselines, and the description of 2604.04651 must be corrected. 'Adapter on for keys, off for reading' is a deployment choice, not a new mechanism. What is untested and project-specific is whether a NIGHTLY PERSONAL sleep LoRA, which already recalls 91% of names, gives better diary keys than a second retrieval round or a cheap alias table. That matters most in the case where hop 1 survives only in weights. The project's router (memory if p>=0.5 else diary, a bad result at 57-60) picked one source instead of chaining them. This test chains them, against fair rivals.

SCOPE: small K2-3.7B Week-2 fact world only, kept separate from the village model and the card experiments.

PRE-CHECK (no GPU): find the results file behind 'base reads diary 84.6 vs slept 66'. The advisor could not find it by grep. If it is not found, the test still runs, because arm D1 (slept reader) against D0 (base reader) measures it directly, but the claim is not quoted until then.

TASK MATCHING REAL USE. Ben asks a question about his own past whose answer needs two facts said on different days ('what's the name of my sister's dentist?'). The assistant has its day-by-day diary (FTS5 over the raw synthetic chats of the Week-2 world) and its slept LoRA.

DATA SOURCE (Claude Batches). 150 cross-day two-hop items (grep-confirmed that no single diary turn holds both hops), each in 2 phrasings: (a) lexical-gap-filtered (no rare token shared with the source turns), (b) natural, written as Ben would ask, with no filter. Plus 200 one-hop items, 50 never-taught items (the right answer is 'don't know'), and an optional 50 items Ben writes himself about the synthetic week (reported, not gating). CONDITION W: for 75 of the 150 two-hop items, the hop-1 turn is deleted from the index AFTER sleep. Every serve-side component, including D4's alias table, sees only the post-deletion diary; the LoRA was trained before deletion. Grading is exact match after NFKC; a Haiku grader via Batches handles answer variants (Sonnet spot-check of 60, kappa reported). Diagnostics are logged: bridge named correctly, and hit@3 for each hop.

ARMS. The same ab_ob_b4_nb LoRA (seeds 1 and 2, existing checkpoints, or retrained at about 1.2 T4-h each if missing), the same 1.5k k_tokens, and a base LoRA-off reader unless noted:
- D0: BM25(question) only.
- D1: the same, with the slept reader.
- D2: base writes a closed-book 40-token key pass (plain query expansion).
- D3 (EQUAL-COMPUTE baseline): two-round retrieval. Base reads the round-1 hits and writes 40-token bridge keys; round 2 uses BM25 on question+keys, then RRF and trimming. Same decode budget (40 key tokens), same number of retrieval rounds (2), same final k_tokens as R. D3 prefills more (round-1 hits), which favours the baseline.
- D4: nightly alias/entity table built by Claude Batches from the diary, used for zero-decode query expansion. It uses more API compute than R, which also favours the baseline.
- R: slept LoRA-on key pass, LoRA-off read.
- R+D3: slept keys added to round 2 (are the two complementary?).
- Ablation: R with a tau gate tuned on a 30-item dev split. It does not count toward the pass marks.
SEEDS: 2.

METRICS. Accuracy per split; bridge-named rate; hit@3 for hop 1 and hop 2; 'don't know' rate on never-taught items; on the M1 Pro (K2 q4, mlx), added wall-clock per memory question including the second prefill, and the decode tok/s of 3 other agents while key passes run.

PASS MARKS (fixed in advance; paired McNemar per item, pooled over 2 seeds; the sign must hold in each seed):
1. Natural-phrasing cross-day two-hop: R >= max(D3, D4) + 8 points, p < 0.05.
2. Condition W: R >= max(D3, D4) + 15 points, p < 0.05.
3. One-hop: R >= D0 - 1.
4. Never-taught 'don't know': R >= D0 - 5.
5. Mac: added wall-clock per memory question <= 1.5 s; the other agents' tok/s drop <= 10% while key passes run.
Passes 1-5 make R adoptable and let stage 2 be pre-registered. Pass 2 alone, with 1 failing, means 'keep only as a fallback when diary search misses'.

RESULT THAT PROVES IT WRONG: R - max(D3, D4) < 3 on natural phrasing AND < 8 on condition W. Sleep-as-key-writer then adds nothing over a second retrieval round or an alias table; the idea is dropped, stage 2 included. DIAGNOSTIC: if R names the right bridge on more than 80% of items but two-hop accuracy stays below 50%, the bottleneck is the reader; stop and work on reading.

COMPUTE PLAN (Kaggle T4x2, vLLM with per-request LoRA). 7 arms + 1 ablation x about 625 items (300 two-hop phrasings + 75 W + 200 + 50) x 2 seeds, short decodes (40 + about 20 tokens), 1.5k prefill: about 1.5 GPU-h. Building the FTS5 index and W deletions is CPU work. If the LoRAs must be retrained: +2.4 GPU-h. TOTAL about 1.5-4 GPU-h. Mac latency and multi-agent check: about 30 min on the M1 Pro. API via Batches: items and phrasings about $1.5, D4 tables about $0.5, grading about $1. TOTAL about $3.

judged.plain_summary:
Ben, here is the short version. Eight ideas were checked, and two are worth testing first.

Pick 1, "Ask once, then remember": each night the assistant looks at today's mistakes. One kind is when it guessed and you had to correct it. The other is when it asked you something it already knew. It then practises asking in the first kind of situation and acting in the second. The fair rival is a version that just keeps a small note of your past answers and is told "ask if something is missing". That rival gets exactly the same amount of night training, just on other examples. The test asks one question: does the night practice make it better at spotting brand-new ambiguities, like a "Sam" it has never met, without pestering you on clear requests? If the note-only version does just as well, we keep the note and skip the training. It costs about 5 hours of free Kaggle GPU and about $5 of Claude, and it is only run in a fake test world for now. If you have a week of real assistant logs, we first check that you actually make enough corrections for this to learn from.

Pick 2, "Recall-then-read": for questions like "what's my sister's dentist called?", the trained memory writes a few search words ("sister = Maya") and the untrained model reads what the diary search finds. It must beat two simpler tricks: searching twice, and a ready-made "who is who" list. It matters most when the original diary entry is gone and only the trained memory still knows the link. It needs no new training, about 2-4 GPU-hours.

The other six were set aside, either because a much cheaper trick probably does the same job or because they cost too much to test fairly right now. Every pass mark is fixed in advance, and each plan says which result would show the idea is wrong.
